question: Why does this project encrypt a whole entry (title + username + password + notes) as a single AES-256-GCM blob instead of encrypting each field separately?
answer_hinglish:
Yahan decision hai: entry ka EK blob, alag-alag encrypted fields nahi. Reasoning README aur PLAN.md mein likha hai -- is project mein koi requirement nahi hai ki vault unlock kiye bina title ya username se search/sort karna ho. Agar aisi requirement hoti, tab shayad title ko separately encrypt karna fayda deta taaki index bana sako. Par yahan ek hi use hai: unlock karo, phir sab decrypt karke dikhao.

Agar fields alag encrypt karte, toh har field ka apna IV aur apna ciphertext hota -- matlab har write par 4 IVs generate karna, 4 auth tags manage karna, aur sabko ek saath sync rakhna. Ek chhota sa bug (ek field update hua, doosra IV reuse ho gaya) pura AES-GCM security model tod sakta hai, kyunki same key ke saath IV reuse karna is the ONE way AES-GCM badly breaks.

manager.ts ke addEntry mein dekho: `encrypt(session.key, Buffer.from(JSON.stringify(body), "utf8"))` -- body ek object hai jisme title, username, password, notes, breached sab ek saath JSON ban kar encrypt hote hain, ek IV ke saath. Same updateEntry mein bhi: jab bhi kuch change hota hai, PURA blob fresh IV ke saath re-encrypt hota hai, chahe sirf notes hi badla ho.

Trade-off clear hai: simplicity aur kam attack surface mila, par cost yeh hai ki listEntries ko bhi har entry decrypt karna padta hai sirf title/username dikhane ke liye -- koi "encrypted index" nahi hai.
why_needed: Interviewer dekhna chahta hai ki candidate samajhta hai field-level vs record-level encryption ka trade-off, aur yeh bhi ki IV reuse kyun itna dangerous hai AES-GCM mein.
real_world_analogy: Ek sealed envelope mein sab documents ek saath daal do vs har document ko alag chhota envelope dena -- pehla simple hai aur kam seals manage karni padti hain, par agar tumhe sirf ek document dikhana ho toh pura envelope kholna padega.
how_it_works: encrypt() har call par naya randomBytes(IV_LENGTH) generate karta hai, isliye single-blob design mein bhi IV reuse ka risk nahi hai -- woh risk tab aata jab multiple fields SAME IV use karte per write, jo yahan hota hi nahi kyunki har field alag call hoti.
in_this_project: src/manager.ts ke addEntry/updateEntry mein DecryptedEntryBody (title, username, password, notes, breached) ek object ban kar JSON.stringify hota hai aur ek hi encrypt() call se EncryptedBlob banta hai -- src/crypto.ts ka EncryptedBlob shape (iv, ciphertext, authTag).
advantages: Ek IV, ek auth tag per write -- kam state manage karna
Field-level sync bug ka risk khatam (sab fields ek atomic unit hain)
Code simple: encrypt/decrypt ek hi call
disadvantages: listEntries ko har entry decrypt karna padta hai sirf title/username dikhane ke liye
Sirf notes update karne par bhi pura blob re-encrypt hota hai
Vault unlock kiye bina kabhi search/sort possible nahi
common_mistakes: Field-level encryption karte waqt same IV sab fields ke liye reuse kar lena
Yeh sochna ki splitting fields se security better ho jaati hai -- yahan koi gain nahi hai jab tak search requirement na ho
Partial update par poora blob dobara encrypt karna bhool jaana (stale blob reh jaana)
follow_up_questions: What would change in this design if you needed to search entries by title without unlocking the vault first?
Why is a fresh IV generated on every updateEntry call, even for an unchanged password?
What is the actual security consequence of reusing an IV under the same AES-GCM key?

question: Why did this project choose RSA-OAEP (hybrid/envelope encryption) for sharing an entry between two independent vaults, instead of hand-rolling an ECIES-style scheme on an elliptic curve?
answer_hinglish:
README ke design choices section mein yeh explicitly likha hai: RSA-OAEP chuna gaya kyunki Node ka built-in crypto module directly `publicEncrypt`/`privateDecrypt` deta hai -- koi extra key-derivation logic likhne ki zaroorat nahi. ECIES (elliptic curve wala approach) mein tumhe khud ECDH karna padta, phir ek KDF (HKDF jaisa kuch) use karke shared secret se symmetric key banani padti, phir uska authentication bhi sambhalna padta -- yeh sab code hai jo galat likha ja sakta hai.

Trade-off yeh hai: RSA keypair generate karna slow hai (2048-bit key banane mein roughly 200ms lagta hai), jabki EC keypair generation bahut fast hota hai. Par yahan yeh cost sirf ONE TIME hai, aur lazy hai -- `getSharingPublicKey` sirf pehli baar call hone par keypair banata hai, har `createVault` par nahi. Toh ek project jo "correct, well-understood implementation" ko prioritize kar raha hai raw speed ke upar, uske liye yeh reasonable trade hai.

Actual flow src/sharing.ts mein hai: `sealForRecipient` ek one-time AES-256 key banata hai (`randomBytes(32)`), entry ka content us AES key se AEAD encrypt karta hai (jaisa project mein har jagah hota hai), aur fir sirf us CHHOTE AES key ko RSA-OAEP se recipient ke public key se wrap karta hai -- `publicEncrypt({ key: recipientPublicKeyPem, oaepHash: "sha256", padding: ... }, oneTimeKey)`. Yeh exactly wahi pattern hai jo TLS aur PGP use karte hain: asymmetric crypto sirf small payload (key) ke liye, bulk data symmetric se.
why_needed: Interviewer yeh dekhna chahta hai ki candidate samajhta hai hybrid encryption kyun zaroori hai (RSA chhota payload hi encrypt kar sakta hai) aur library-provided primitive vs hand-rolled crypto ka risk trade-off.
real_world_analogy: Ek bada parcel (entry content) ko ek chhoti combination-lock chaabi (one-time AES key) se lock karo, phir usi chaabi ko ek bank locker (recipient's RSA public key) mein daal do -- bank ka locker system khud nahi banana padta, Node ka built-in RSA locker use kar lete hain.
how_it_works: sealForRecipient: randomBytes(32) one-time AES key -> encrypt(oneTimeKey, plaintext) AES-256-GCM se -> publicEncrypt(recipientPublicKeyPem, oneTimeKey) RSA-OAEP se. openAsRecipient: privateDecrypt se oneTimeKey nikalta hai, phir decrypt() se plaintext.
in_this_project: src/sharing.ts ka RSA_OPTIONS constant (`oaepHash: "sha256", padding: constants.RSA_PKCS1_OAEP_PADDING`) aur generateSharingKeyPair 2048-bit modulusLength use karta hai. manager.ts ka getSharingPublicKey lazily yeh keypair banata hai, sirf ek baar per vault.
advantages: Node ka publicEncrypt/privateDecrypt directly milta hai -- koi custom KDF/HMAC logic likhne ka risk nahi
Well-understood, widely audited primitive (same pattern TLS/PGP use)
Lazy, one-time keypair generation -- cost sirf sharing use karne wale vaults par
disadvantages: RSA-2048 keypair generation ~200ms synchronous -- EC keypair generation se dheema
RSA-OAEP payload size limited hai, isliye hybrid encryption zaroori hai (extra indirection)
RSA keys EC keys se bade hote hain (token mein zyada bytes)
common_mistakes: RSA se directly bada plaintext encrypt karne ki koshish karna (payload size limit bhool jaana)
Apna ECIES scheme likhna aur usme KDF ya authentication galat karna
Keypair ko createVault par eagerly generate karna, jabki sirf sharing use karne walon ko hi iski zaroorat hai
follow_up_questions: Why can RSA-OAEP not encrypt the entry's full content directly?
What would change if you used an elliptic curve (ECIES-style) scheme instead -- what extra logic would you now own?
Why is the keypair generated lazily instead of at createVault time?

question: Why is session idle expiry checked lazily (only when requireSession runs) instead of with a scheduled background sweep that proactively evicts idle sessions?
answer_hinglish:
Yeh decision PLAN.md ke stage 6 mein explicitly diya hai: lazy expiry is project ke har aur time-based check ke saath consistent hai -- lockout cooldown bhi lazy check hota hai, `SESSION_INVALIDATED` (generation mismatch) bhi lazy hai. Koi background timer kahin nahi hai is project mein.

Reasoning simple hai: ek background sweep job har session ko walk karega, check karega idle hai ya nahi, aur evict karega -- yeh EXTRA code hai ek guarantee ke liye jiski yahan zaroorat hi nahi. Koi bhi idle session, jab tak uska use nahi hota, kisi ko harm nahi kar raha -- woh sirf memory mein baithi hai. Jab tak koi usko actually use karne ki koshish kare, tab tak check karna kaafi hai.

`requireSession` is project ka EK choke point hai jahan se har session-based call guzarta hai -- isliye idle timeout ka check wahi laga diya gaya, aur SAME jagah success par `lastActivityAt` reset hota hai. Koi doosri jagah ko yaad rakhne ki zaroorat nahi ki idle clock check/reset kare.

Ek IMPORTANT design detail: `isSessionActive` ek PURE READ hai -- yeh idle status batata hai par khud clock ko reset NAHI karta. Agar yeh reset kar deta, toh koi caller `isSessionActive` ko poll-poll karke session ko hamesha zinda rakh sakta tha, jo pure feature ko defeat kar deta. Yeh test `session-idle-timeout.test.ts` mein specifically 'polling isSessionActive does NOT itself reset the clock' se verify hota hai.
why_needed: Interviewer samajhna chahta hai ki candidate lazy vs eager expiry ka trade-off samajhta hai, aur yeh bhi ki ek status-check API khud state ko mutate nahi karni chahiye.
real_world_analogy: Office ka light sensor -- koi bijli company har 5 second mein check nahi karti ki light on hai ya nahi, bas jab tum switch dabate ho tab hi check hota hai ki timeout ho gaya ya nahi; aur sirf 'kya light on hai' poochna khud light ko wapas on nahi kar deta.
how_it_works: requireSession(): generation check (SESSION_INVALIDATED) -> idle check `now - lastActivityAt > sessionIdleTimeoutMs` (SESSION_IDLE_TIMEOUT, session delete ho jaati hai) -> success par `lastActivityAt = now()`. isSessionActive(): same checks but return boolean, never mutates.
in_this_project: src/manager.ts ka requireSession method -- single choke point. isSessionActive separate, pure read. test/session-idle-timeout.test.ts mein 9 tests, including 'polling isSessionActive does NOT itself reset the clock' aur 'two sessions on one vault have independent idle clocks'.
advantages: Ek choke point, koi doosri jagah ko remember karne ki zaroorat nahi
Koi background timer/job nahi -- kam moving parts
isSessionActive polling se session ko artificially zinda nahi rakh sakta
disadvantages: Idle session memory mein baithi rehti hai jab tak koi use/check na kare
Agar koi session kabhi use hi nahi hota, woh memory mein forever reh sakta hai is project ki current form mein
Metrics/monitoring ke liye 'abhi kitne sessions idle hain' jaanna harder hai bina ek sweep ke
common_mistakes: isSessionActive ko bhi lastActivityAt reset karne dena -- isse feature hi defeat ho jaata
Idle check ko sirf kuch call sites par lagana, requireSession jaisa single choke point na banana
Background sweep likhna jab project ki scale ko uski zaroorat hi nahi
follow_up_questions: What would happen if isSessionActive also reset lastActivityAt?
At what scale would a lazy-only idle check become a real memory problem, and what would you add then?
Why does requireSession check generation before checking idle timeout?

question: Why does this project pin Express 4 instead of Express 5, and what does that force asyncRoute() to do?
answer_hinglish:
README aur PLAN.md dono mein yeh decision likha hai: Express 4 chosen hai, EXACTLY `21-notification` project ki pinned version match karne ke liye -- is repo ke across-projects consistency zyada matter karti hai kisi ek project ke apna stack choose karne se. Aur yahi decision hai jiski wajah se `asyncRoute()` function exist karta hai.

Problem yeh hai: Express 4 khud kisi rejected promise ko automatically error-handling middleware tak route NAHI karta. Matlab agar tumne ek async route handler likha jo throw/reject karta hai, aur usko Express 4 directly diya, toh request HANG ho jaayegi -- koi response kabhi nahi jaayega, koi error bhi nahi. Express 5 mein yeh automatically ho jaata hai.

Isliye http/app.ts mein `asyncRoute()` wrapper likha gaya: jo bhi route `PasswordManager` ka ek ASYNC method call karta hai (addEntry, updateEntry, deleteEntry, getSharingPublicKey, redeemShare, changeMasterPassword, checkBreach), uska handler ek `.catch(next)` ke saath wrap hota hai -- taaki rejection Express ke error-handling middleware tak pahunche.

Jo routes SYNCHRONOUS method call karte hain (createVault, unlock, shareEntry, revokeShare), unko asyncRoute ki zaroorat NAHI, kyunki Express 4 already ek synchronous throw ko sahi se route kar leta hai -- sirf PROMISE rejection ka hi masla hai. Mutation check H7 ne isi ko real prove kiya: `.catch(next)` hata do, async route ka error hang ho jaata hai response bheje bina.
why_needed: Interviewer dekhna chahta hai ki candidate Express ki promise-handling history samajhta hai aur yeh bhi ki 'consistency across repo' bhi ek valid architecture decision hoti hai.
real_world_analogy: Purani car mein manual gear hai -- clutch khud dabana padta hai (asyncRoute wrapper), naye automatic car (Express 5) mein yeh khud ho jaata hai. Dono jagah pahunch sakte ho, par purani car mein ek extra step yaad rakhna padta hai.
how_it_works: asyncRoute(handler) returns (req, res, next) => handler(req, res).catch(next) -- woh .catch(next) hi Express 4 ki missing automatic rejection-routing ki jagah leta hai.
in_this_project: src/http/app.ts ka asyncRoute function; isko POST /sessions/:sessionId/entries, PATCH .../entries/:entryId, DELETE .../entries/:entryId, GET .../sharing-key, POST .../shares/redeem, POST /vaults/:ownerId/rotate, POST /breach-check -- har jagah jahan manager ka async method call hota hai, wrap karne ke liye use hota hai. Mutation H7 'asyncRoute's .catch(next) removed' is exact behavior ko test karta hai.
advantages: Consistency across this repo's HTTP layers (same version as 21-notification)
asyncRoute() ek single, testable wrapper hai -- har route ko apna try/catch nahi likhna padta
Forgetting asyncRoute on a sync route causes no bug, since Express 4 already handles sync throws
disadvantages: Har async route handler ko manually asyncRoute() mein wrap karna yaad rakhna padta hai
Express 5 upgrade karne par yeh wrapper technically unnecessary ho jaata (though harmless)
Ek developer naya async route add karke asyncRoute bhool sakta hai -- request hang ho jaayegi
common_mistakes: Ek naye async route par asyncRoute() wrapper lagana bhool jaana
Sync route par bhi asyncRoute laga dena jab zaroorat na ho (harmless but unnecessary)
Yeh sochna ki Express version upgrade kiye bina hi rejected promises automatically handle ho jaayengi
follow_up_questions: What would actually happen to a client's request if asyncRoute's .catch(next) were removed?
Which routes in this project do NOT need asyncRoute, and why?
If this project upgraded to Express 5, would asyncRoute become unnecessary or just redundant?

question: Why does this project write its own small, self-contained CircuitBreaker in src/circuit-breaker.ts instead of importing a resilience library from this repo's other resilience-themed projects (18-resilience, 19-rate-limit)?
answer_hinglish:
README ke design choices section mein yeh decision clearly diya hai: is repo ka har project apna standalone package hai -- koi cross-project runtime dependency nahi. Aur breach-check ke liye jo circuit breaker chahiye, woh kaafi CHHOTA hai (closed/open/half-open, bas teen states) -- usko directly likhna (`timeout.ts`/`withTimeout` jaisa simple module) ek cross-project dependency wire karne se SIMPLER hai.

Trade-off yahan hai: duplication vs coupling. Agar `18-resilience` se breaker import karte, toh ek shared dependency ban jaati -- kal `18-resilience` mein koi change hoga toh is project ka behavior bhi silently badal sakta hai, aur is project ka 'npm ci, npm test' standalone chalna band ho jaata agar sibling project ka build fail ho. Chhoti functionality ke liye itna coupling introduce karna worth nahi hai.

Actual implementation src/circuit-breaker.ts mein hai: `run<T>(fn)` -- agar state 'open' hai aur cooldown abhi nahi guzra, `CIRCUIT_OPEN` error throw karta hai BINA `fn()` ko call kiye (fail-fast, same philosophy jaisa vault ke claims mein hai). Success par `consecutiveFailures = 0` aur state 'closed'. Failure par counter badhta hai; threshold hit hone par ya half-open trial fail hone par state 'open' ho jaata hai.

Yeh breaker phir `BreachChecker` (src/breach-checker.ts) mein `withTimeout` ke saath combine hota hai: `this.breaker.run(() => withTimeout(..., this.timeoutMs))`. Mutation checks ne isko thoroughly validate kiya -- CB2 jaisa bug (success failure counter reset nahi karta) genuinely pakda gaya tha, isi se pata chalta hai ki yeh 'simple' breaker bhi testing ke bina subtle bugs chhupa sakta hai.
why_needed: Interviewer samajhna chahta hai ki candidate monorepo mein dependency-sharing ka trade-off samajhta hai -- kab shared library sahi hai, kab har project ko apna chhota implementation rakhna better hai.
real_world_analogy: Ek chhoti startup apni khud ki chhoti utility function likh leti hai instead of ek bada third-party framework import karne ke, kyunki uski zaroorat sirf 20 lines ki hai -- par ek bade company mein shared library use karna sense banta hai kyunki duplication ka cost zyada hota hai multiple teams ke across.
how_it_works: CircuitBreaker.run(fn): open+cooldown-elapsed -> half-open trial; open+cooldown-not-elapsed -> throw without calling fn(); success -> reset counter, close; failure -> increment counter, open if threshold hit or half-open trial failed.
in_this_project: src/circuit-breaker.ts ka CircuitBreaker class, DEFAULT_FAILURE_THRESHOLD=3, DEFAULT_COOLDOWN_MS=10000. src/breach-checker.ts ka BreachChecker isko withTimeout ke saath wrap karta hai. test/circuit-breaker.test.ts mein 6 tests including half-open trial ka cooldown-after-failure reset.
advantages: No cross-project runtime dependency -- this project stays fully standalone
Small enough (3 states, ~40 lines) that writing it directly is lower risk than wiring an import
Easy to test in isolation with ManualClock, no shared library's test setup needed
disadvantages: Duplication: if 18-resilience already has a well-tested breaker, this project re-implements similar logic
No shared bug-fixes: a bug fixed in the other repo's breaker does not automatically help this one
Every resilience-themed project in this repo maintains its own slightly different breaker
common_mistakes: Importing a cross-project dependency for a small amount of logic, coupling builds unnecessarily
Forgetting that a success must reset consecutiveFailures (mutation CB2's exact bug)
Calling fn() even while the circuit is open instead of failing fast
follow_up_questions: At what point would you actually promote this to a shared library across projects?
What would change if the breach-check provider started being called from multiple unrelated features?
How does the half-open state differ in risk from simply closing the circuit after the cooldown?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Shared library import karte toh ek version-coupling problem create hoti -- is project ka test suite dusre project ke code par depend karta, aur ek breaking change dusre project mein yahan silently test fail kar sakta tha. Standalone chhota implementation rakhne se yeh coupling zero hai, cost sirf thoda duplication hai -- ek acceptable trade jab logic itna small ho.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Agar breach-check provider consistently slow ho jaaye (network degradation), breaker open ho jaata hai aur agle calls fast-fail karte hain null return karke, bina provider ko hit kiye -- save kabhi block nahi hota. Agar breaker khud buggy ho (jaisa CB2 mutation dikhata hai), toh ek false sense of protection mil sakta hai jab asal mein counter kabhi reset hi nahi ho raha.
advanced.alternatives: Ek shared `18-resilience`/`19-rate-limit` library import karna; ya ek generic npm package (opossum jaisa) use karna jo production-grade metrics/events bhi deta. Trade-off: zyada features par ek external dependency jo is project ki 'zero runtime dependency in the library' promise todti.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: 10x breach-check calls par: single in-process breaker fine rehta hai agar sab calls same process mein ho rahe hain. 100x par, agar multiple PasswordManager instances alag processes mein chal rahe hain (horizontal scaling), har instance ka apna ALAG breaker state hoga -- ek instance ka circuit open hoga, doosra abhi bhi closed, jo inconsistent degradation dikhayega. Real production mein ek SHARED circuit state (Redis-backed) chahiye hoga cross-instance coordination ke liye.
advanced.production_improvements: Metrics/alerting add karna jab circuit open ho (abhi sirf getState() hai, koi event emit nahi hota). Half-open trial ko sirf ek request tak limit karna explicitly document/test karna multiple concurrent half-open calls ke against. Agar scale badhe, shared/distributed circuit state consider karna taaki saare instances consistent decision lein.

question: Why do share grants live in a manager-wide shares map instead of being stored inside each VaultRecord?
answer_hinglish:
README aur PLAN.md stage 5 mein yeh reasoning diya hai: ek share grant VAULT CONTENT nahi hai -- yeh METADATA hai ek transaction ke baare mein jo DO vaults ke beech ho raha hai (sender aur recipient). Yeh same reasoning hai jo already `sessions` ko manager-level par rakhta hai, per-vault nahi.

Agar `shares` ko `VaultRecord` ke andar rakhte, toh pehla sawal yeh hota: kiske VaultRecord mein? Sender ke, kyunki usne share banaya? Ya recipient ke, kyunki wahi ise redeem karega? Dono galat hain -- share grant dono se independent hai, aur VaultStore ke through persist hona wrong hoga kyunki yeh encrypted content nahi hai, bas bookkeeping hai (shareId, ownerId, revoked, redeemedAt).

Actual implementation: `private readonly shares = new Map<string, ShareGrant>()` manager class level par, EXACTLY jaise `sessions` map hai. `shareEntry` call par ek naya grant register hota hai (`this.shares.set(shareId, {...})`), `revokeShare` isi map mein `revoked = true` set karta hai, `redeemShare` isi map mein `redeemedAt` set karta hai -- single-use ke liye claim-before-await.

Kyunki yeh manager-wide map hai aur VaultStore se bypass karta hai, yeh README ke 'Known and NOT handled' section mein already documented limitation ka hissa hai: shares registry restart survive nahi karti, exactly sessions jaisa. Design ne isi trade-off ko explicitly accept kiya -- consistency within the codebase (same pattern, same limitation) was preferred over giving shares their own persistence story.
why_needed: Interviewer dekhna chahta hai ki candidate samajhta hai 'data ownership' ka sawal -- kaunsa data KISKA hai, aur transaction-metadata vs content ka distinction kaise architecture decisions drive karta hai.
real_world_analogy: Bank mein ek money-transfer receipt kisi ek account ke andar nahi file hoti -- woh bank ki apni central transaction log mein hoti hai, kyunki yeh dono accounts ke BEECH ki ek event hai, kisi ek ka exclusive record nahi.
how_it_works: shareEntry registers a ShareGrant in the manager-wide shares map (not inside sender's VaultRecord). revokeShare and redeemShare both look it up by shareId from that same map, independent of either vault's own storage.
in_this_project: src/manager.ts ke PasswordManager class mein `private readonly shares = new Map<string, ShareGrant>()`, bilkul `sessions` jaisa. ShareGrant interface: shareId, ownerId (only this vault may revoke), revoked, redeemedAt. test/share-revocation.test.ts mein 7 tests isi grant ke lifecycle ko cover karte hain.
advantages: Correctly models a grant as metadata ABOUT a transaction, not content belonging to either vault
Consistent with the existing sessions-map pattern -- one fewer design to learn
No ambiguity about which vault 'owns' a share record
disadvantages: Does not survive a restart (same documented limitation as sessions) -- an issued, unredeemed share is lost if the process restarts
A manager-wide map grows unboundedly without any cleanup of old redeemed/revoked grants
Not backed by VaultStore, so there is no durability story for shares at all in this project
common_mistakes: Putting the share grant inside the sender's VaultRecord and then having to decide arbitrarily which vault owns it
Forgetting that redeemShare's claim must be synchronous, before any await, to prevent double redemption
Treating an unknown shareId and someone else's shareId as different errors (leaks existence)
follow_up_questions: What would change if shares needed to survive a process restart in production?
Why must revokeShare report an unknown shareId and someone-else's shareId identically?
How would you add an expiry cleanup for old redeemed or revoked shares without a background sweep?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Manager-wide map metadata-vs-content separation ko clean rakhta hai, par cost yeh hai ki shares ka koi persistence path nahi hai -- VaultStore sirf vault content ke liye hai. Ek alternative design mein shares ke liye apna chhota 'ShareStore' banaya ja sakta tha, jo durability deta par ek extra abstraction layer add karta.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Process restart hone par saari pending (unredeemed) shares silently gayab ho jaati hain -- sender ko pata bhi nahi chalega ki unka issued share ab kaam nahi karega jab tak recipient redeem try na kare aur UNKNOWN_SHARE paaye. Yeh confusing hai production mein agar documented na ho.
advanced.alternatives: Shares ko VaultStore ke through persist karna (par phir kis vault ke saath associate karna confusing hai); ek alag ShareStore banana jo ismein specialize ho; ya shares ko ek external service (jaisa Redis TTL key) mein rakhna jo naturally expiry bhi handle kar de.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: 10x shares par in-memory Map fine rehta hai single process mein. 100x+ scale par, agar multiple PasswordManager instances horizontally scaled hain, shares map per-instance ho jaata hai -- ek instance par issued share doosre instance par redeem nahi ho sakta jab tak koi shared store (Redis/DB) na ho. Yeh exact same scaling problem hai jo sessions ko bhi hogi.
advanced.production_improvements: Shares ko ek shared, TTL-capable store (Redis) mein move karna taaki multi-instance deployment mein kaam kare aur crash-survive kare. Explicit expiry on time add karna (abhi sirf revocation/single-use hai, koi time-based expiry nahi -- README mein yeh gap documented hai). Periodic cleanup of old redeemed/revoked entries to bound memory growth.

question: This project's VaultStore is entirely in-memory and nothing survives a restart (not even the sessions and shares registries). What would actually need to change to deploy this as a real, restart-surviving password manager service?
answer_hinglish:
README ka 'Known and NOT handled' section seedha bolta hai: 'Everything is in memory, one process... nothing survives a restart -- including the shares grant registry and session idle clocks.' VaultStore interface khud design mein hi 'a real disk/network backend could be dropped in' ke liye bana hai, par abhi sirf InMemoryVaultStore hai jo `Promise.resolve()` ke baad snapshot ko ek Map mein save karta hai.

Real deployment ke liye sabse pehla kaam: VaultStore interface implement karna ek real database ke saath (Postgres, DynamoDB, ya koi encrypted-at-rest store) -- `persist(snapshot: PersistedVault, signal: AbortSignal)`. snapshot mein already sirf ciphertext hai (salt base64, canary EncryptedBlob, entries ka blob) -- plaintext kabhi bhi store ke paas nahi jaata, toh yeh part already sahi design hai, sirf backend badalna hai.

Doosra bada issue: `sessions` aur `shares` maps purely in-memory hain, VaultStore se bypass karte hain. Production mein yeh ek fast key-value store (Redis) mein jaana chahiye -- restart survive karne ke liye AUR multi-instance deployment ke liye bhi (agar ek se zyada process chal rahe hain, in-memory Map har instance ka alag hoga).

Teesra: vault LOOKUP abhi `this.vaults.get(ownerId)` in-memory hai -- yeh bhi backing store se load hona chahiye, probably ek cache layer ke saath (scrypt itself slow hai, isliye derived key cache karna bhi matter karta hai, par master password kabhi cache mein nahi jaana chahiye). Startup par existing vaults ko kahin se bhi 'load' karne ka koi path abhi code mein nahi hai -- yeh add karna hoga.

Chautha: commitTimeoutMs aur withTimeout ka design already real network latency ke against ready hai (STORE_TIMEOUT), jo acha sign hai ki is layer ko swap karna conceptually straightforward hoga.
why_needed: Interviewer dekhna chahta hai ki candidate samajhta hai 'in-memory prototype to production service' ka real gap, aur yeh bhi recognize kare ki design (VaultStore abstraction, ciphertext-only snapshots) already is migration ko easy banata hai.
real_world_analogy: Ek startup ne pehle apna prototype ek whiteboard par record rakha (in-memory) -- jaise hi woh real customers ke liye launch karte hain, unhe woh records ek fireproof filing cabinet (durable database) mein move karna padta hai, bina records ka FORMAT badle (ciphertext already sahi format mein hai).
how_it_works: VaultStore.persist(snapshot, signal) is the one seam: swap InMemoryVaultStore for a real implementation talking to a durable backend, and vault/session/share lookups need an equivalent durable-or-cached load path.
in_this_project: src/store.ts ka VaultStore interface aur InMemoryVaultStore class -- yahi seam hai. src/manager.ts ke constructor mein `this.store = options.store ?? new InMemoryVaultStore()` -- dependency injection already is swap ko supports karta hai bina manager.ts ko chhuye.
advantages: VaultStore interface is already dependency-injected, so swapping backends needs no change to manager.ts
Snapshots are ciphertext-only -- the real backend never needs to be trusted with plaintext
withTimeout/AbortSignal already models real network latency against the store
disadvantages: sessions and shares maps bypass VaultStore entirely and would need a separate durability story
No vault-loading path exists today -- a cold-start process has zero vaults until createVault is called again
Caching derived keys for performance would need very careful design so the master password itself is never cached
common_mistakes: Assuming swapping VaultStore alone makes the whole system restart-safe (sessions/shares are a separate gap)
Caching the derived master-password key insecurely, defeating the point of scrypt's cost
Loading all vaults into memory eagerly at startup instead of lazily or on demand
follow_up_questions: Would you load every vault into memory at startup, or lazily on first access -- what are the trade-offs?
How would you handle a session or share surviving a restart without ever persisting a plaintext key?
What changes in the claim/commit model if the store can partially fail (e.g. write succeeds but the acknowledgment is lost)?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: VaultStore ko swap karna low-risk hai (already abstracted), par sessions/shares ko durable banane ka decision bada architectural choice hai: ek shared cache (Redis) add karna ek NAYI dependency hai jo abhi project ke 'zero runtime dependency in the library' promise ko todti -- yeh trade-off explicitly accept karna padega production ke liye.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Process crash hone par: vault content safe hai (agar real VaultStore use kiya) kyunki har commit already durable thi; par har active session/share grant gayab ho jaata hai -- users ko dobara unlock karna padega, aur in-flight shares redeem nahi ho paayenge. Partial write failure (store commit crash ke beech) ka risk bhi hai agar real backend ACID guarantees na de.
advanced.alternatives: Postgres/DynamoDB jaisa durable store entries ke liye; Redis sessions/shares ke liye TTL ke saath; ya ek event-sourced design jahan har mutation ek append-only log mein jaaye aur vault state us log se rebuild ho (zyada complex, par better audit trail).
advanced.scale_10x_100x: 10x vaults par, ek simple key-value store (vault per ownerId) still kaam karega. 100x+ par, ownerId se sharding/partitioning chahiye hoga, aur InMemoryVaultStore jaisa 'ek Map' approach clearly impossible ho jaata hai -- real database indexing aur connection pooling zaroori ban jaate hain.
advanced.production_improvements: Real durable VaultStore implementation add karna (sabse pehla kaam). Sessions/shares ko Redis jaisi fast, TTL-capable store mein move karna. Startup par vault-loading strategy design karna (lazy-on-demand recommended, eager load avoid karna bade datasets ke liye). Backup/restore process define karna using exportVault's existing ciphertext-only shape.

question: README's 'Known and NOT handled' section lists no CORS, no rate limiting beyond the vault's own lockout, and no 2FA. Which of these would you prioritize first for a real deployment, and why?
answer_hinglish:
Teeno gaps README mein explicitly documented hain: 'The HTTP API has no CORS, no per-end-user session/cookie layer, and no rate limiting of its own' aur 'No 2FA, no password-strength scoring beyond the generator's own charset rules.' Priority decide karne ke liye yeh dekhna padega ki HTTP API kis TRUST BOUNDARY par baithi hai.

Yeh API 'authenticates SERVICES, not end users, with one bearer API key' -- PLAN.md isko explicitly kehta hai. Matlab yeh browser ke saamne directly expose nahi karne ke liye design hui hai -- isliye CORS actually kam urgent hai jab tak koi browser-based client isko direct call na kar raha ho. Agar deployment is scope mein hi rahe (service-to-service), CORS largely irrelevant hai.

Sabse pehle main RATE LIMITING ko fix karunga, kyunki vault ka own lockout sirf WRONG PASSWORD attempts ko limit karta hai -- ek attacker jo different ownerIds try kar raha hai, ya valid session ke saath hi flood kar raha hai, is project ke lockout se completely untouched hai. Yeh ek transport-layer concern hai jo already README mein flagged hai, aur easy hai ek reverse proxy (nginx/API gateway) ya Express middleware se add karna, bina library ko touch kiye.

Uske baad 2FA -- yeh master password ke upar ek extra factor add karta hai, important for real user accounts, par is project ka scope seva-authentication hai (API key), end-user authentication alag layer hai jo iske upar banegi. Isliye yeh teesra priority, kyunki yeh pehle se hi ek alag architectural layer ka kaam hai (jaisa README bolta hai, 'a real deployment would put this behind its own backend').
why_needed: Interviewer dekhna chahta hai ki candidate security gaps ko BLINDLY list nahi karta, balki trust boundary aur deployment context ke hisaab se priority deta hai.
real_world_analogy: Ek internal company API jo sirf backend services call karte hain usko CORS ki zaroorat nahi (browsers kabhi usse directly baat nahi karte), par rate limiting zaroori hai taaki ek buggy ya malicious caller pura system flood na kar de.
how_it_works: The HTTP API's only protection today is one bearer API key (constant-time compared) plus the library's own per-vault lockout after MAX_FAILED_ATTEMPTS wrong unlock attempts -- neither covers cross-ownerId request flooding.
in_this_project: src/http/app.ts ka createApp sirf ek API-key middleware lagata hai, koi rate-limiting middleware nahi. src/manager.ts ka verifyMasterPassword lockout sirf ek ownerId ke wrong-password attempts ko count karta hai, cross-owner flooding ko nahi.
advantages: Rate limiting can be added at the gateway/middleware level without touching the library
The existing lockout already protects against single-owner password guessing
The API's service-to-service scope narrows which gaps are actually urgent
disadvantages: A single persistent attacker hitting many different ownerIds is not covered by anything today
Adding CORS/2FA/rate limiting all at the HTTP layer risks duplicating logic across services if not centralized
No audit trail for who is calling the API with the shared key -- a compromised key cannot be revoked per-caller
common_mistakes: Treating this HTTP API like a public, browser-facing API and adding CORS before rate limiting
Assuming the library's lockout covers cross-owner request flooding (it does not)
Building 2FA directly into this library instead of recognizing it belongs to the end-user auth layer above it
follow_up_questions: Where exactly would you put rate limiting -- in this Express app, or in front of it at a gateway?
What would change about this priority list if the API were ever exposed directly to browsers?
How would you design per-caller API key revocation given today's single shared key?

question: This project has no directory service for exchanging sharing public keys -- callers get the recipient's public key out of band. What would you build to fix that for production, and what security property would it have to preserve?
answer_hinglish:
README explicitly likhta hai: 'No directory service for exchanging public keys. Callers are responsible for getting the recipient's public key to the sender out of band; this project does not model how that handoff happens.' Code mein `getSharingPublicKey(sessionId)` sirf CALLER ke apne vault ka public key return karta hai -- kahin bhi 'dave ka public key alice ko do' jaisa koi lookup-by-ownerId function nahi hai.

Production fix: ek simple directory service -- ek endpoint jaisa `GET /vaults/:ownerId/sharing-key` (session ke bina, kyunki public key koi secret nahi hai) jo kisi bhi ownerId ka current sharing public key return kare. Yeh safe hai dena kyunki `generateSharingKeyPair`'s public key 'not secret, safe to hand to anyone' hai -- comment mein yeh explicitly likha hai sharing.ts mein.

Par SABSE IMPORTANT security property jo preserve karni hai: yeh directory service sirf PUBLIC key expose kare, kabhi private key ya koi encrypted blob nahi. Aur dusra bada risk: MAN-IN-THE-MIDDLE -- agar directory service compromise ho jaaye aur attacker apna public key 'dave ka public key' bana ke de de, toh alice unknowingly attacker ke liye seal kar degi. Isliye real production mein yeh directory ek trusted, authenticated endpoint hona chahiye (jaisa HTTPS + certificate pinning, ya ek key-fingerprint verification step out-of-band jahan user khud confirm kare).

Ek doosra consideration: key rotation. Agar koi vault apna sharing keypair kabhi rotate kare (abhi project mein yeh feature nahi hai -- keypair sirf once lazily generate hota hai), directory service ko stale keys serve karne se bachna hoga.
why_needed: Interviewer dekhna chahta hai ki candidate public-key infrastructure ka basic trust model samajhta hai -- public key share karna safe hai, par WHO gives you that key ka trust zaroor matter karta hai (MITM risk).
real_world_analogy: WhatsApp jaisa app jab tumhe kisi ka public key automatically deta hai, woh bhi ek trust decision hai -- isliye WhatsApp 'security code verify karo' jaisa out-of-band check deta hai taaki tum confirm kar sako ki yeh really wahi person ka key hai, kisi attacker ka nahi.
how_it_works: A directory endpoint would expose VaultRecord.sharingPublicKey (lazily generated by getSharingPublicKey) by ownerId, never touching wrappedPrivateKey, and would need its own transport trust (TLS) plus some out-of-band verification step to defeat MITM substitution.
in_this_project: src/manager.ts ka getSharingPublicKey sirf caller's OWN vault ke liye hai (requires an active session). src/sharing.ts's generateSharingKeyPair comment explicitly marks publicKey as 'not secret, safe to hand to anyone' -- that is the property a directory service would rely on.
advantages: A directory endpoint removes the manual out-of-band key exchange burden on callers
Public keys are safe to expose by design -- no new secret is created by this service
Simple to add as a read-only, unauthenticated-by-session endpoint keyed only by ownerId
disadvantages: A compromised directory service could substitute an attacker's public key (MITM on the handoff)
No key rotation story exists today to build a directory around
Adds an availability dependency: sharing now depends on this service being up
common_mistakes: Exposing wrappedPrivateKey or any encrypted blob through the directory service instead of just the public key
Trusting the directory service blindly without any out-of-band verification step for the recipient's identity
Forgetting the directory service needs its own authentication for WRITES (publishing a key) even if reads are open
follow_up_questions: How would you let a user verify they got the correct public key for a recipient, without a full PKI?
What changes in this design if sharing keypairs could be rotated?
Would you authenticate reads from this directory service, and if so, how?

question: The HTTP API authenticates with one shared bearer API key for the whole service. How would this evolve to serve multiple independent tenants as a real multi-tenant SaaS deployment?
answer_hinglish:
Abhi ka model PLAN.md mein explicit hai: 'The HTTP API authenticates SERVICES, not end users, with one bearer API key -- the same scope 21-notification's API has.' Code mein `createApp`'s auth middleware ek SINGLE `expected` digest ke against constant-time compare karta hai -- koi tenant concept hi nahi hai, sab callers ek hi trust level par hain.

Multi-tenant SaaS banane ke liye sabse pehla change: API key EK se MULTIPLE ban jaani chahiye, har ek ek tenant/caller se associated ho, aur request ke andar yeh pata chalna chahiye 'yeh request KISKI taraf se hai.' `keyMatches` function ko redesign karna hoga -- ek single Buffer compare karne ke jagah, ek lookup (key -> tenantId) chahiye, phir bhi timing-safe tareeke se (ek naive loop-and-compare timing attack leak kar sakta hai ki kitne keys exist karte hain).

Doosra bada change: DATA ISOLATION. Abhi `ownerId` flat hai -- `vaults.get(ownerId)`. Multi-tenant mein, ownerId collisions bachaane ke liye isko `tenantId:ownerId` jaisa namespace karna hoga, ya tenant ko ek alag field bana ke har lookup mein pass karna. Agar yeh na kiya jaaye, ek tenant doosre tenant ke vault access kar sakta hai sirf same ownerId guess karke -- yeh ek real security bug hoga.

Teesra: rate limiting aur quotas PER TENANT honi chahiye, na ki globally -- abhi toh koi rate limiting hi nahi hai (already documented gap), par jab add karenge tab per-tenant buckets chahiye honge taaki ek noisy tenant doosron ko affect na kare. Aur logging/metrics ko bhi per-tenant tag karna hoga taaki billing aur debugging possible ho.

Chautha: key management lifecycle -- key rotation, revocation per-tenant, aur ek admin API jahan se naye tenant onboard ho sakein, sab naya infrastructure hai jo abhi exist nahi karta.
why_needed: Interviewer samajhna chahta hai ki candidate single-tenant se multi-tenant jaane ka REAL cost samajhta hai -- sirf auth badalna kaafi nahi, data isolation aur per-tenant resource fairness bhi chahiye.
real_world_analogy: Ek building jisme pehle ek hi master key sab kholti thi, ab usko apartments mein convert kar rahe ho -- har tenant ko apni alag chaabi chahiye, AUR ek tenant ki chaabi doosre ka apartment nahi khol paani chahiye, chahe woh building staff ho.
how_it_works: keyMatches today does one timingSafeEqual against one expected digest. A multi-tenant version needs a lookup from presented key to tenantId (still timing-safe), plus that tenantId flowing through to every manager call that touches ownerId-scoped state.
in_this_project: src/http/app.ts ka keyMatches function aur app.use auth middleware -- single `expected` Buffer. src/manager.ts ka vaults Map is keyed purely by ownerId with no tenant dimension at all today.
advantages: Per-tenant keys allow independent revocation without affecting other tenants
Tenant-scoped data isolation prevents one tenant from touching another's vaults by ownerId collision
Per-tenant rate limiting and metrics become possible once a tenantId exists on every request
disadvantages: Significant new infrastructure: key management, tenant onboarding, per-tenant quotas
Every ownerId-keyed lookup in PasswordManager needs rethinking for tenant scoping
More attack surface: a buggy tenant-scoping check is a direct cross-tenant data leak
common_mistakes: Adding per-tenant keys but forgetting to also namespace ownerId, leaving cross-tenant collisions possible
Comparing presented keys with a non-constant-time lookup, leaking timing information about how many keys exist
Applying rate limits globally instead of per-tenant, letting one tenant starve the rest
follow_up_questions: How would you keep the key comparison timing-safe once there are many possible keys instead of one?
Where exactly would tenantId need to be threaded through PasswordManager's public API?
How would you migrate existing single-tenant data into a tenant-scoped model without downtime?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Tenant scoping ko HTTP layer mein hi handle karna (ownerId ko tenantId:ownerId bana ke) vs PasswordManager ko khud tenant-aware banana -- pehla approach library ko unchanged rakhta hai (simpler), par ownerId namespacing ek leaky abstraction hai jo HTTP layer ko manually maintain karni padegi. Doosra approach cleaner hai par library ka API surface badal deta hai.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Agar tenant-scoping bug ho jaaye (jaisa namespace prefix lagana bhool jaana ek route mein), ek tenant doosre tenant ka vault directly access kar sakta hai -- yeh worst-case data breach hai multi-tenant SaaS mein. Key-lookup bhi agar naive ho (array loop with early-exit compare), timing attack se key existence leak ho sakta hai.
advanced.alternatives: Row-level security jaisa pattern database layer mein enforce karna (agar real DB backend ho) taaki application-layer bug bhi data leak na kare. Ya har tenant ko apna ALAG PasswordManager instance dena (full isolation, par resource-heavy at scale).
advanced.scale_10x_100x: 10x tenants par ek shared PasswordManager instance with namespaced ownerIds still practical hai. 100x+ tenants aur high-traffic tenants ke saath, noisy-neighbor problem real ban jaata hai -- per-tenant rate limiting, aur potentially per-tenant sharding of the backing store, zaroori ho jaate hain taaki ek bada tenant chhote tenants ko slow na kare.
advanced.production_improvements: Per-tenant API keys with a secure lookup/rotation system. Tenant-scoped data model (either namespacing or a tenantId column in a real DB). Per-tenant rate limiting and usage metrics for billing. Database-level isolation (row-level security or per-tenant schemas) as a defense-in-depth layer beyond application code.

question: In production, callers will get VAULT_BUSY or ENTRY_CONFLICT under real concurrent load, and this library does no automatic retry (a documented limitation). How would you design the retry/backoff and idempotency strategy for a client sitting in front of this API?
answer_hinglish:
README bolta hai: 'No automatic retry on VAULT_BUSY/ENTRY_CONFLICT. The caller is told someone else got there first and must decide whether to retry; this project does not do that for them.' Yeh deliberate design hai -- library apna claim-before-await machinery use karke sirf 'kisne pehle claim kiya' decide karti hai, retry policy ek HIGHER-LEVEL concern hai jo caller/gateway ka kaam hai.

Retry design ke liye pehla sawal: KAUN SA operation retry-safe hai? `VAULT_BUSY` (claimEntryOp mein, ya changeMasterPassword ke rotating/pendingEntryOps check mein) matlab operation ne KUCH NAHI kiya -- yeh error means nothing happened ka part hai, isliye yeh bilkul safely retry kiya ja sakta hai, EXPONENTIAL BACKOFF ke saath (kyunki contention hi iska cause hai, immediate retry sirf contention badhayega).

`ENTRY_CONFLICT` thoda different hai -- yahan DO writes conflict hui, aur loser ka kaam discard ho gaya. Yahan BLIND retry galat hai: agar caller sirf wahi purana patch dobara bhej de, woh ab stale data ke upar likh raha hai. Correct approach hai: GET entry dobara (fresh version lene ke liye), merge/re-apply user's intended change us fresh state par, phir retry karo. Yeh essentially optimistic-concurrency-control ka standard pattern hai -- `version` field already is design mein hai, caller isko expose karke apne retry logic mein use kar sakta hai.

Idempotency ke liye: `addEntry` jaisa call agar client-side retry ki wajah se dobara bheja jaaye (network timeout ke baad, par pehla call actually succeed ho gaya tha), tab duplicate entry ban jaayegi -- is project mein koi idempotency key field nahi hai is operation ke liye (`21-notification` project mein hai, par yahan nahi). Production client ko apna khud ka idempotency key generate karna chahiye aur ek dedupe-check layer gateway par rakhna chahiye, ya is library mein addEntry ko ek optional idempotencyKey parameter dena chahiye.

`STORE_TIMEOUT` ek alag category hai -- yeh pata nahi hai ki commit actually succeeded ya nahi (store se confirmation nahi mila). Yahan retry karna RISKY hai bina idempotency ke, kyunki ho sakta hai pehla attempt actually land kar gaya ho.
why_needed: Interviewer dekhna chahta hai ki candidate samajhta hai ki har error code ka retry-safety ALAG hoti hai -- blanket 'retry on any 409' ek naive aur potentially dangerous approach hai.
real_world_analogy: ATM se paisa nikalte waqt agar transaction 'pending' dikhaye aur connection cut jaaye, tum dobara card daal ke SEEDHA wahi amount firse nikalne ki koshish nahi karte -- pehle balance check karte ho ki pehla transaction hua ya nahi, phir decide karte ho.
how_it_works: VAULT_BUSY means nothing happened (safe to retry with backoff); ENTRY_CONFLICT means the loser's work was discarded (must re-fetch fresh state before retrying); STORE_TIMEOUT means the outcome is genuinely unknown (needs idempotency to retry safely).
in_this_project: src/manager.ts ka claimEntryOp aur changeMasterPassword ke VAULT_BUSY throws; updateEntry ka version-based ENTRY_CONFLICT check; src/timeout.ts ka withTimeout jo STORE_TIMEOUT produce karta hai jab commit deadline cross kare.
advantages: Keeping retry policy out of the library keeps it simple and lets each deployment choose its own policy
Per-error-code retry semantics map cleanly onto the library's own 'an error means nothing happened' documentation
The existing version field already supports an optimistic-concurrency-based client retry strategy
disadvantages: Every client of this library must independently implement correct retry logic -- a real risk of inconsistent handling
No built-in idempotency key support for addEntry/shareEntry means client-side retries can create duplicates
STORE_TIMEOUT's genuinely-unknown-outcome case is the hardest to retry safely without additional support
common_mistakes: Blindly retrying ENTRY_CONFLICT with the exact same stale patch instead of re-fetching first
Retrying STORE_TIMEOUT without any idempotency guard, risking a duplicate write
Retrying immediately without backoff, which only increases contention under real load
follow_up_questions: How would you add an idempotency key to addEntry without breaking its existing claim/commit shape?
What backoff strategy would you use for VAULT_BUSY specifically, given what causes it?
How would a client safely determine the true outcome of a request that failed with STORE_TIMEOUT?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Retry logic library ke andar bake karna vs caller/gateway par rakhna -- library mein rakhte toh ek consistent policy milti par flexibility kam ho jaati (har deployment ki retry needs alag ho sakti hain). Caller par rakhna flexible hai par consistency ka risk hai agar har client team apna alag (potentially buggy) retry likhe.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Ek naive client jo blindly har 409 par same request retry kare -- VAULT_BUSY par theek chalega (safe), par ENTRY_CONFLICT par stale data overwrite kar dega agar woh fresh GET na kare. STORE_TIMEOUT par blind retry duplicate entries bana sakta hai bina idempotency key ke.
advanced.alternatives: Library ke andar hi ek optional idempotencyKey parameter add karna addEntry ko (jaisa 21-notification karta hai apne notify() call ke liye) -- yeh har client ko apna retry-safety khud reinvent karne se bachata. Ya ek thin client SDK banana jo retry/backoff policy ko encapsulate kare.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: 10x load par occasional VAULT_BUSY/ENTRY_CONFLICT normal hai aur naive retry-with-backoff kaam karta hai. 100x+ load par, same vault par high contention (bahut saare devices ek vault ko simultaneously hit kar rahe hain) exponential backoff ko bhi struggle karwa sakta hai -- yahan client-side request COALESCING ya queueing consider karna padega taaki redundant retries na ho.
advanced.production_improvements: addEntry/shareEntry mein optional idempotencyKey support add karna. Client SDK/wrapper banana jo per-error-code retry policy ko encapsulate kare. STORE_TIMEOUT ke baad outcome-verification endpoint (jaisa 'getEntry by a client-known reference') provide karna taaki retry decide karna aasan ho.

question: Walk through the entire claim-before-await concurrency pattern in this project end to end: where it is used, what invariant it guarantees, and why it works without a lock.
answer_hinglish:
Yeh pattern is pure project ki backbone hai, aur yeh teen alag jagah use hota hai, har jagah ek alag resource ko protect karte hue, par EXACT SAME shape mein: SYNCHRONOUS claim, phir ek `await`, phir synchronous apply ya release.

Stage 2 mein `claimEntryOp(record)`: entry operations (addEntry/updateEntry/deleteEntry/getSharingPublicKey) call karne par pehla kaam hota hai -- `if (record.rotating) throw VAULT_BUSY; record.pendingEntryOps++;` -- yeh SYNCHRONOUSLY chalta hai, koi await ke pehle. Isi tarah `changeMasterPassword` apna claim leta hai: `if (record.rotating) throw; if (record.pendingEntryOps > 0) throw; record.rotating = true;`. Dono claims ek doosre ko exclude karte hain -- ek rotation aur ek entry-op kabhi same vault par EK SAATH in-flight nahi reh sakte.

Stage 5 mein `redeemShare` isi shape ko DOOSRE resource (share grants) ke liye reuse karta hai: `share.redeemedAt = this.clock.now();` -- yeh claim hai, await se pehle. Is wajah se do concurrent redemptions ek hi token ke liye kabhi dono succeed nahi kar sakte.

Yeh KYUN kaam karta hai bina kisi lock library ke: JavaScript ka execution model single-threaded hai, aur synchronous code KABHI preempt nahi hota beech mein. Jab `claimEntryOp` chal raha hai, koi doosra code EK SAATH nahi chal sakta -- function call khatam hone tak JS engine kuch aur execute nahi karega. Isliye 'claim' atomic hai BY CONSTRUCTION, koi mutex ya compare-and-swap ki zaroorat nahi.

AWAIT ke baad, jab control wapas aata hai, state badal chuki ho sakti hai (koi doosra claim ban gaya ho). Isliye commit ke BAAD bhi re-check hota hai -- jaisa `updateEntry` mein `current.version !== expectedVersion` check. Aur `finally` block mein claim RELEASE hoti hai (`record.pendingEntryOps--`), chahe commit succeed ho ya throw kare -- taaki ek failed commit vault ko permanently 'busy' na chhod de.
why_needed: Yeh is project ka single sabse important architectural idea hai -- interviewer yahan dekhna chahta hai ki candidate samajhta hai ki JS ka single-threaded model concurrency control ke liye kaise leverage hota hai bina traditional locks ke.
real_world_analogy: Ek single bank teller jisko ek customer ke saath pehle ek chhota form fill karna hota hai (synchronous claim) -- jab tak teller yeh form fill kar raha hai, koi doosra customer BEECH mein nahi aa sakta, yeh atomicity teller ke 'one thing at a time' nature se aati hai, koi security guard (lock) ki zaroorat nahi. Phir teller ek async cheque-clearing process ke liye bank ke peeche jaata hai (await), aur wapas aa kar form complete karta hai.
how_it_works: Pattern: synchronous claim (throws if excluded) -> one await across the store/async call -> synchronous apply on success or release on failure, always in a finally for release-style claims.
in_this_project: src/manager.ts: claimEntryOp (stage 2, entries vs rotation), changeMasterPassword's rotating=true claim, redeemShare's share.redeemedAt claim (stage 5). test/concurrency.test.ts has a dedicated illustration of the UNGUARDED version of the bug this prevents, for contrast.
advantages: No lock library or database transaction needed -- correctness is a property of JS's execution model
Same reusable shape applies to any new race-prone resource (entries, rotation, share grants)
Claims and releases are both trivially testable with a FakeVaultStore that controls exact interleaving
disadvantages: Relies on JS's single-threaded guarantee -- would not directly translate to a genuinely multi-threaded runtime
Each new mutable resource needs its own claim counter/flag, which is manual bookkeeping, not a generic primitive
A forgotten release (missing finally) would permanently wedge the claim for that resource
common_mistakes: Putting any await BEFORE the claim, which reopens the exact race the pattern exists to prevent
Forgetting to release the claim in a finally, leaving VAULT_BUSY forever after one failure
Assuming this pattern would still work correctly if ported to a genuinely multi-threaded environment unchanged
follow_up_questions: What would break if claimEntryOp's increment happened after an await instead of before?
How would you adapt this pattern for a resource shared across multiple Node processes, not just one?
Why does redeemShare's NO_SHARING_KEY check happen before the claim, not after?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Construction-based exclusion (claim-before-await) vs a traditional lock/mutex library: the former needs zero extra dependencies and is trivially correct given JS's execution model, but it only protects a SINGLE process's in-memory state -- it gives you nothing across processes, which a real distributed lock would.
advanced.failure_scenarios: If a claim is ever taken but its release path is skipped (a missing finally, or an exception that escapes before the try block), the vault gets permanently stuck reporting VAULT_BUSY for every future call -- the project's own mutation checks (S6, S7) specifically probe for exactly this kind of gap.
advanced.alternatives: A real mutex/semaphore library; a database-level row lock or optimistic version column (which this project already partially uses via the entry `version` field) ; or a distributed lock (Redis-based) if this needed to work across multiple processes.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: Within one process, this pattern scales fine regardless of request volume -- contention just means more VAULT_BUSY rejections, which is a correct, cheap outcome. The moment this runs as MULTIPLE processes (horizontal scaling), the entire pattern stops working: rotating/pendingEntryOps/sessions all live in one process's memory, so two processes could both believe they hold the only claim on the same vault.
advanced.production_improvements: For a single-process deployment, this pattern needs no change. For horizontal scaling, the claim state (rotating, pendingEntryOps, share redemption) would need to move to a shared, atomically-updatable store (Redis with atomic INCR/compare-and-set, or a database row with optimistic locking), replacing the in-memory counters with a cross-process equivalent of the same claim-before-await shape.

question: Walk through the full envelope-encryption sharing flow end to end: from shareEntry on the sender's vault to redeemShare on the recipient's vault, naming every key involved.
answer_hinglish:
Yeh flow DO independent vaults ke beech hai, aur poora point yeh hai ki kabhi bhi dono vaults ek doosre ka master password, vault key, ya private key nahi dekhte.

Step 1 (recipient side, pehle se): recipient (dave) `getSharingPublicKey(dave.sessionId)` call karta hai. Agar dave ne pehle kabhi sharing use nahi ki, yeh LAZILY ek naya RSA-2048 keypair banata hai (`generateSharingKeyPair`), uska privateKey dave ke APNE vault key se encrypt karta hai (`encrypt(session.key, Buffer.from(privateKey, "utf8"))`), aur commit karta hai. Public key return hoti hai -- yeh secret nahi hai, dave isko alice ko out-of-band deta hai.

Step 2 (sender side): alice `shareEntry(alice.sessionId, entryId, davePublicKey)` call karti hai. Yeh ek PURE SYNCHRONOUS function hai -- koi commit nahi, kyunki alice ke vault mein kuch badal nahi raha. Pehle apne OWN vault key se entry decrypt karti hai (`decryptBody(session.key, stored.blob)`), phir `sealForRecipient(davePublicKey, plaintext)` call karti hai: ek fresh one-time AES-256 key banta hai, entry content us key se AES-GCM encrypt hota hai, aur SIRF us chhote AES key ko dave ke public key se RSA-OAEP wrap kiya jaata hai. Result: `{ wrappedKey, blob }`. Manager level par ek `shareId` generate hota hai aur ek grant register hota hai `shares` map mein.

Step 3 (recipient redeems): dave `redeemShare(dave.sessionId, token)` call karta hai. Pehle checks: UNKNOWN_SHARE, SHARE_REVOKED, SHARE_ALREADY_REDEEMED, NO_SHARING_KEY -- sab claim se PEHLE. Phir claim: `share.redeemedAt = now()`. Dave apni OWN wrappedPrivateKey ko apne vault key se decrypt karta hai, `openAsRecipient(privateKeyPem, token)` call karta hai -- yeh RSA-OAEP se one-time key nikalta hai, phir uss key se AES-GCM blob decrypt karta hai, plaintext milta hai.

Step 4: woh plaintext seedha dave ke APNE `addEntry()` ko pass hota hai -- matlab yeh entry dave ke vault mein EXACTLY wahi claim/commit exclusion aur breach-check (DAVE ke configuration ke against, alice ke nahi) se guzarti hai jaisi koi normal manually-typed entry guzarti. Agar koi step fail ho (wrong key, tampered token, VAULT_BUSY), claim catch block mein release ho jaati hai taaki real retry ka ek legitimate chance mile.
why_needed: Interviewer yeh dekhna chahta hai ki candidate hybrid encryption ka COMPLETE lifecycle samajhta hai, saare keys ko trace kar sakta hai, aur exclusion/breach-check reuse ka reasoning bhi de sakta hai.
real_world_analogy: Ek sealed parcel bhejna jisme asli saaman (entry) ek chhoti combination lock (one-time AES key) se locked hai, aur us lock ka combination ek doosre, recipient-only bank locker (RSA public key) mein daal diya gaya hai -- parcel khud khareedna, lock karna, bank locker mein combination daalna, yeh sab SENDER karta hai; bank se combination nikalna aur parcel kholna RECIPIENT karta hai, apne private access se.
how_it_works: shareEntry: decrypt(senderKey, entry) -> sealForRecipient(recipientPublicKey, plaintext) -> {wrappedKey, blob} + shareId grant. redeemShare: claim -> decrypt(recipientKey, wrappedPrivateKey) -> openAsRecipient(privateKeyPem, token) -> plaintext -> addEntry(recipientSession, plaintext).
in_this_project: src/manager.ts::shareEntry and ::redeemShare; src/sharing.ts::sealForRecipient and ::openAsRecipient. test/sharing-integration.test.ts covers the full round trip between two independent vaults including the token never containing plaintext in the clear.
advantages: Neither vault ever learns the other's master password, vault key, or private key
redeemShare reuses addEntry wholesale, so sharing gets the exact same claim/commit/breach-check guarantees as any normal entry
shareEntry needs no commit at all, since nothing about the sender's vault changes
disadvantages: A share token is a self-contained artifact with no expiry on time -- only revocation or single-use redemption ends it
No directory service means the public key handoff (alice getting dave's key) is entirely out of band
If the sender's own vault is later deleted or rotated incorrectly, existing unredeemed tokens still work (they do not depend on the sender afterward)
common_mistakes: Checking NO_SHARING_KEY after claiming the share grant instead of before, which would burn a precondition failure's one-time use
Forgetting that shareEntry is synchronous and needs no commit -- adding one would be unnecessary and wrong
Re-checking breach status against the sender's configuration instead of the recipient's own, inside redeemShare
follow_up_questions: Why does redeemShare call addEntry instead of writing its own insertion logic?
What happens if the recipient's own addEntry hits VAULT_BUSY midway through redeemShare?
Why is shareEntry synchronous while redeemShare is async?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Making shareEntry a self-contained, portable token (vs a live call between two vaults) trades off real-time control (sender cannot un-send after handoff, only revoke the grant) for simplicity (no network call needed between two independent PasswordManager instances at share-creation time).
advanced.failure_scenarios: If the recipient's own addEntry fails partway through redeemShare's call (e.g. VAULT_BUSY), the share claim is released so the recipient gets a genuine second chance -- but if the FAILURE itself were misclassified as success (a bug), the share would be burned with nothing actually added, locking the recipient out of ever redeeming it.
advanced.alternatives: A live, synchronous handshake between two PasswordManager instances instead of a portable token -- would need both vaults' managers reachable at the same time, losing the 'send now, redeem later' flexibility this design has.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: At 10x shares, the manager-wide shares map is still fine in one process. At 100x+ shares across many vaults, or across multiple PasswordManager instances, the shares map (like sessions) becomes a cross-instance consistency problem -- a share created on instance A must be redeemable on instance B, which requires a shared store, not an in-memory Map.
advanced.production_improvements: Add an explicit time-based expiry on shares (today only revocation and single-use end them). Move the shares registry to a shared, durable store for multi-instance deployments. Build a real public-key directory service with an out-of-band verification step to remove the manual key handoff and its MITM risk.

question: Explain the design of the error-code-to-HTTP-status mapping in src/http/app.ts -- why does every PasswordManagerErrorCode get its own specific status, and what is 500 reserved for?
answer_hinglish:
README mein explicitly likha hai: 'Every PasswordManagerErrorCode maps to a specific HTTP status; none of them maps to 500 -- every one is an expected, documented outcome, and 500 is reserved for a genuine bug.' Yeh ek deliberate design philosophy hai: library ka HAR error code ek KNOWN, anticipated situation represent karta hai, isliye HTTP layer ko bhi usko ek specific, meaningful status dena chahiye -- generic 400/500 ek lazy design hoti.

`STATUS_BY_CODE` ek `Record<PasswordManagerErrorCode, number>` hai jo TypeScript compile-time par hi guarantee karta hai ki har code ka mapping exist kare -- agar koi naya error code `errors.ts` mein add ho aur `STATUS_BY_CODE` mein mapping bhool jaaye, TypeScript compile hi nahi hoga. Yeh ek 'exhaustiveness check' hai jo runtime bug ko compile-time error bana deta hai.

Mapping ka logic semantically sahi hai: 404 (`UNKNOWN_OWNER`, `UNKNOWN_ENTRY`, `UNKNOWN_SHARE`) jahan resource hi exist nahi karta; 409 (`VAULT_ALREADY_EXISTS`, `VAULT_BUSY`, `ENTRY_CONFLICT`, `NO_SHARING_KEY`, `SHARE_ALREADY_REDEEMED`) jahan request VALID hai par current state ke saath conflict kar rahi hai; 410 SPECIFICALLY `SHARE_REVOKED` ke liye -- yeh HTTP semantics ka proper use hai: resource THA, ab explicitly GONE hai, 404 se semantically different hai; 423 `LOCKED_OUT` ke liye (resource locked); 503 `STORE_TIMEOUT` ke liye (service temporarily unavailable, retry-worthy); 401 jahan authentication/session proof fail hui (`INVALID_MASTER_PASSWORD`, `UNKNOWN_SESSION`, `SESSION_INVALIDATED`, `SESSION_IDLE_TIMEOUT`).

`toHttp` function error ko THREE buckets mein classify karta hai: `HttpError` (HTTP layer ne khud throw kiya, jaisa auth ya Content-Type check), `PasswordManagerError` (library se aaya, STATUS_BY_CODE se map hota hai, default 500 agar koi naya code mapping mein miss ho jaaye -- defensive fallback), aur BAAKI SAB (body-parser errors by `type` field, aur truly unexpected errors) -- yeh LAST category hi 500 paata hai, aur `log()` ke through server-side logged hota hai, kabhi caller ko internal detail leak nahi hota.
why_needed: Interviewer dekhna chahta hai ki candidate HTTP status code semantics ko deeply samajhta hai, aur yeh bhi recognize kare ki 'error handling design' khud ek first-class architecture decision hai, afterthought nahi.
real_world_analogy: Ek hospital ka triage system -- har symptom ko ek SPECIFIC department route kiya jaata hai (fracture -> orthopedics, chest pain -> cardiology), generic 'go see a doctor' nahi diya jaata; aur agar koi TRULY unprecedented symptom aaye jiski category hi nahi pata, TABHI usko emergency/general ward (500 ka equivalent) mein bheja jaata hai.
how_it_works: toHttp(error): HttpError -> its own status/code; PasswordManagerError -> STATUS_BY_CODE[code] ?? 500; body-parser type-tagged errors -> 400/413/415; anything else -> logged and 500.
in_this_project: src/http/app.ts ka STATUS_BY_CODE Record and toHttp function; mutation check H5 ('a status-code mapping entry wrong') specifically validated this table is correct for every code.
advantages: TypeScript's Record type makes a missing mapping a compile error, not a silent runtime gap
Callers can switch on the specific error code AND get a semantically correct HTTP status for generic HTTP tooling
500 is reserved purely for truly unexpected bugs, never leaking internal detail for documented outcomes
disadvantages: Adding a new PasswordManagerErrorCode always requires a matching STATUS_BY_CODE entry -- an extra step developers must remember (though TypeScript enforces it)
Some codes share a status (e.g. several map to 409), so a caller relying ONLY on the HTTP status loses some distinction that the `code` field preserves
The ?? 500 fallback in toHttp is only a safety net -- if it is ever actually hit, it means the exhaustiveness guarantee was bypassed somehow
common_mistakes: Mapping a documented, expected error to 500 instead of a specific status
Forgetting that the error body's `code` field exists precisely so callers do not have to infer meaning from the HTTP status alone
Using 404 for SHARE_REVOKED instead of 410, losing the 'it existed, now it's gone' semantic distinction
follow_up_questions: Why is SHARE_REVOKED mapped to 410 instead of 404, and why does that distinction matter to a caller?
What would happen today if a new PasswordManagerErrorCode were added without updating STATUS_BY_CODE?
Why does the auth middleware's HttpError never go through PasswordManagerError's mapping table?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: A single exhaustive Record keeps the mapping centralized and type-checked, at the cost of needing every new error code to immediately decide its HTTP status before it can even compile -- a tighter coupling between the library's error vocabulary and the HTTP layer's status vocabulary than a looser, runtime-only mapping would have.
advanced.failure_scenarios: If a genuinely new, unanticipated PasswordManagerErrorCode somehow bypassed the TypeScript exhaustiveness check (e.g. through an `as any` cast or a library version mismatch), toHttp's `?? 500` fallback would mask it as a generic internal error, hiding what is actually a well-understood, documented outcome from the caller.
advanced.alternatives: A looser design where PasswordManagerError itself carries its own suggested HTTP status (set at throw time) instead of a separate lookup table -- removes the risk of the two getting out of sync, but couples the pure library to HTTP semantics it should not need to know about.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: This mapping's cost is O(1) per request regardless of scale -- it is a pure lookup table, so it does not change with request volume. What DOES matter at scale is consistency: as more error codes and more routes are added, keeping this table accurate depends entirely on the TypeScript exhaustiveness check continuing to be enforced in CI.
advanced.production_improvements: Add a lint rule or CI check that fails if STATUS_BY_CODE and PasswordManagerErrorCode's union type ever diverge (beyond relying on TypeScript alone). Consider exposing a machine-readable error catalog (code -> status -> meaning) as part of the API's own documentation/OpenAPI spec, generated directly from this table so client SDKs stay in sync automatically.

question: If this PasswordManager ran as multiple stateless HTTP instances behind a load balancer instead of one in-process Map, what would break first, and how would you redesign sessions/generation/idle-timeout to survive that?
answer_hinglish:
Abhi `PasswordManager` class ke teeno core maps -- `vaults`, `sessions`, `shares` -- sab EK process ki memory mein hain. Jaise hi tum ek LOAD BALANCER ke peeche DO ya zyada instances chalate ho, pehla cheez jo tootegi: ek device `unlock()` call karega instance A par, `sessionId` paayega, par uska AGLA request load balancer dusre instance B par route kar de -- B ke `sessions` map mein us sessionId ka koi record hi nahi hai. Caller ko `UNKNOWN_SESSION` milega, bina kuch galat kiye.

Doosra, zyada SUBTLE problem: `generation` counter. Yeh vault record ke andar (jo bhi instance ke pass hai) hai -- agar `changeMasterPassword` instance A par chale aur `generation` ko bump kare, par instance B ke apne memory mein PURANA vault record hai jiska generation abhi bhi old value hai, toh B par ek session jo asal mein invalidated hona chahiye tha, VALID treat ho jayega. Yeh ek real security gap hai -- stale session ek instance par abhi bhi 'generation match' dikhayega jab doosre instance ne already rotate kar diya hai.

Teesra: idle-timeout clock bhi per-session, per-process hai -- agar session ka traffic do instances ke beech bounce karta hai, dono ko apna khud ka `lastActivityAt` pata hoga, consistent nahi hoga.

Redesign: vault record, sessions, aur shares SAB ek SHARED, externally-visible store mein jaane chahiye (Redis ya similar) jo ATOMIC read-modify-write support kare. `generation` ek atomic counter banna chahiye wahan -- jab bhi koi instance `requireSession` call kare, usse FRESH generation value padhna hoga shared store se, na ki apni local memory se. Claim-before-await pattern (jaisa `claimEntryOp`) bhi redesign hona padega -- single-process synchronous execution ki guarantee ab nahi hai, isliye ek atomic compare-and-set (Redis `SETNX`/Lua script, ya database row-level lock) chahiye hoga same invariant ke liye jo pehle JS ke single-thread se mil rahi thi.

Yeh essentially ek 'in-memory single-node design' ko 'distributed, shared-state design' mein convert karna hai -- ek bahut bada architectural shift, is library ke current zero-runtime-dependency design ke bilkul opposite direction mein.
why_needed: Interviewer dekhna chahta hai ki candidate samajhta hai ki JS ke single-threaded concurrency guarantees sirf ONE PROCESS tak extend hote hain, aur horizontal scaling ka REAL cost kya hota hai jab state in-memory ho.
real_world_analogy: Ek chhoti dukaan jahan EK hi malik har customer ka order khud yaad rakhta hai (single process memory) -- jaise hi tum branch kholte ho (multiple instances), har branch ka apna alag khata hai; agar customer branch A mein order de aur branch B mein pickup karne jaaye, branch B ko us order ka pata hi nahi hoga jab tak dono branches ek shared central ledger (shared store) na use karein.
how_it_works: Today: sessions/vaults/shares are per-process Maps, generation is a per-record integer in local memory. Multi-instance: all three need to live in a shared store with atomic operations, and generation checks must always read the current shared value, not a per-instance cached copy.
in_this_project: src/manager.ts ka Session interface (`generation: number`, captured at unlock time), VaultRecord's `generation` field bumped by changeMasterPassword, and requireSession's lazy comparison -- all of this today assumes one shared in-memory view across every caller.
advantages: The lazy generation-check design is conceptually easy to port to a shared store -- it is already just an integer comparison
Claim-before-await's INVARIANT (mutual exclusion) is well understood, so the distributed equivalent has a clear target to hit
No change needed to the crypto layer itself -- only to WHERE state (sessions/vaults/shares/generation) lives
disadvantages: Every claim (claimEntryOp, rotating, redeemShare's claim) needs a genuinely atomic distributed equivalent, which is strictly harder to get right than synchronous in-process code
Introduces a new, critical runtime dependency (Redis/DB) that the library currently deliberately avoids
Network round trips to the shared store add latency to every session-based call that previously was a free in-memory lookup
common_mistakes: Adding a load balancer with sticky sessions as a 'fix' without addressing the generation/stale-read problem for ANY cross-instance traffic (failover still breaks it)
Using a non-atomic read-then-write against the shared store for claims, reintroducing the exact race the in-process version prevented
Assuming Redis alone solves consistency without also solving for Redis's own failure modes (e.g. a Redis failover losing recent writes)
follow_up_questions: How would you implement claimEntryOp's atomic claim against a shared store like Redis?
What happens to an in-flight commit if the instance handling it crashes mid-operation in this redesign?
Would you use sticky sessions as a stopgap, and what would it NOT fix?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Keeping PasswordManager in-process and simple (current design) vs making it genuinely distributed -- the former is correct and simple only at single-instance scale; the latter requires accepting network latency and a new dependency (shared store) on every operation that used to be a pure in-memory check, in exchange for actual horizontal scalability.
advanced.failure_scenarios: Without a redesign: a session created on instance A is unusable on instance B (UNKNOWN_SESSION for a perfectly valid session) the moment a load balancer routes without stickiness; a stale generation on one instance can let an invalidated session keep working after a password rotation that another instance already processed -- a real security hole, not just a usability bug.
advanced.alternatives: Sticky sessions at the load balancer (a partial stopgap that still breaks on instance failure/scale-down); a shared Redis/DB-backed session+vault store (the real fix); or a fully different architecture where each vault is pinned to exactly one instance via consistent hashing, keeping the in-memory model but routing traffic to the right instance instead of making state shared.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: At 10x traffic with sticky sessions, this mostly works until any instance restarts or scales down, at which point every session on that instance is lost. At 100x traffic needing real horizontal scale and resilience, a shared store becomes mandatory, and the claim-before-await pattern must be reimplemented as atomic operations against that store (Redis Lua scripts or DB transactions), fundamentally changing the latency profile of every mutating call.
advanced.production_improvements: Move vaults/sessions/shares/generation into a shared, atomically-updatable store. Reimplement claimEntryOp/rotating/redeemShare's claim as atomic compare-and-set operations against that store. Consider consistent-hashing-based routing (pin a vault to one instance) as a lower-risk alternative to full distributed state if traffic patterns allow it.

question: This vault's entries live in a single in-memory Map<string, StoredEntry> per owner, and listEntries decrypts every entry on every call. What breaks first at 10x and 100x the number of entries per vault, or 10x/100x the number of vaults, and how would you redesign storage?
answer_hinglish:
Do alag scaling dimensions hain, aur dono alag jagah tootenge.
