Dimension 1: EK vault ke andar entries ki count badhna. `listEntries` abhi `[...record.entries.values()].map((stored) => this.toSummaryEntry(stored, this.decryptBody(session.key, stored.blob)))` -- yeh HAR entry ko DECRYPT karta hai, chahe caller ko sirf pehli 20 entries dikhani ho. 10x entries (jaise 50 se 500) par shayad noticeable nahi hoga, par 100x (5000+ entries ek vault mein) par yeh ek O(n) decrypt operation ban jaata hai HAR listEntries call par -- scrypt-derived key se AES-GCM decrypt bhale fast ho, par 5000 baar karna real latency add karta hai, especially agar bahut saare concurrent users ho.

Isse bada issue `changeMasterPassword` mein hai: `for (const stored of record.entries.values()) { const body = this.decryptBody(oldKey, stored.blob); reEncrypted.set(...) }` -- yeh EVERY entry ko decrypt+re-encrypt karta hai, PHIR ek SINGLE commit mein poora snapshot store ko bhejta hai. 100x entries par yeh commit ka payload bhi 100x bada ho jaata hai, aur `commitTimeoutMs` (default 5 seconds) us bade commit ke liye kam pad sakta hai -- STORE_TIMEOUT zyada frequently aayega.

Dimension 2: vaults (owners) ki count badhna. `this.vaults = new Map<string, VaultRecord>()` -- SAB vaults EK process ki memory mein, hamesha. 10x owners (jaise 1000 se 10000) toh fine hai, par 100x+ (lakhs of owners) par SAB vaults ko hamesha memory mein rakhna impractical ho jaata hai -- yahan ek real database ke saath LRU-style caching chahiye hoga, vaults ko on-demand load/evict karna, na ki sabko permanently memory mein rakhna.

Redesign: listEntries ko PAGINATED banana (abhi koi pagination nahi hai), aur ideally metadata (title, username, timestamps) ko ek alag, searchable index mein rakhna taaki poora blob decrypt na karna pade sirf list dikhane ke liye -- yeh is project ke 'ek blob per entry' trade-off ka direct consequence hai jo PWD-086 mein discuss hua. changeMasterPassword ko batch commits mein todna (ek commit se poore vault ko re-encrypt karne ke jagah, incremental re-encryption with its own progress tracking) bade vaults ke liye zaroori ho jaayega.
why_needed: Interviewer dekhna chahta hai ki candidate samajhta hai ki 'it works in tests' aur 'it scales' alag baatein hain, aur specific O(n) operations ko identify kar sakta hai jo scale ke saath problem bante hain.
real_world_analogy: Ek chhoti library jahan librarian har baar POORI shelf check karta hai ek kitaab dhundne ke liye -- 100 kitaabon tak theek hai, par 100,000 kitaabon ke saath yeh approach tootega; tabhi ek catalog (index) banane ki zaroorat padti hai jo har kitaab ko bina poori shelf scan kiye dhoondh sake.
how_it_works: listEntries today: O(n) decrypt over every entry in the Map, no pagination. changeMasterPassword today: O(n) decrypt+re-encrypt over every entry, then one commit carrying the entire re-encrypted snapshot.
in_this_project: src/manager.ts::listEntries and ::changeMasterPassword both iterate `record.entries.values()` in full; src/manager.ts's `vaults` Map holds every VaultRecord in process memory with no eviction.
advantages: The current simple design (one Map, one full re-encrypt, one commit) is easy to reason about and already atomic -- no partial rotation state to worry about
A correctness-first design at today's scale avoids premature complexity (pagination, incremental rotation) that this project's own tests do not need
The VaultStore abstraction already decouples the commit shape from any specific backend, so a redesign would not require touching the crypto or claim logic
disadvantages: listEntries has no pagination -- every call decrypts the full entry set regardless of how many the caller actually wants to see
changeMasterPassword's single big commit means its STORE_TIMEOUT risk grows with vault size, with no partial-progress recovery
Holding every vault in memory with no eviction does not scale to a very large number of owners
common_mistakes: Assuming AES-GCM decrypt speed alone determines listEntries' scalability, ignoring the O(n) iteration and JSON parsing cost
Redesigning changeMasterPassword into incremental batches without preserving its all-or-nothing atomicity guarantee
Adding pagination to listEntries without also reconsidering the single-blob-per-entry design that makes title search require full decryption
follow_up_questions: How would you add pagination to listEntries without breaking its current all-decrypted-at-once simplicity?
What would an incremental, resumable changeMasterPassword look like, and what new failure modes would it introduce?
At what entry count would you expect STORE_TIMEOUT's default 5-second budget to start being a real problem?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Keeping the current all-at-once design (simple, atomic, easy to prove correct) vs an incremental/paginated redesign (scales better, but loses the clean all-or-nothing atomicity that changeMasterPassword currently guarantees, and needs new machinery to track partial progress safely).
advanced.failure_scenarios: At high entry counts, a changeMasterPassword commit that exceeds commitTimeoutMs fails with STORE_TIMEOUT -- and because the whole operation is all-or-nothing, the user must retry the ENTIRE rotation from scratch, which could repeatedly fail if the vault is consistently near the timeout boundary, effectively locking the user out of ever rotating their password.
advanced.alternatives: Move entry metadata (title, username, timestamps) into a separate, lightly-indexed structure that listEntries can read without decrypting the full blob, while keeping the sensitive blob encryption as-is; or make changeMasterPassword incremental with a resumable cursor and its own progress-tracking state (at the cost of a more complex failure model than today's atomic commit).
advanced.scale_10x_100x: 10x entries per vault: listEntries and changeMasterPassword get noticeably slower but likely still correct and within timeout. 100x entries per vault, or 100x more vaults: listEntries' lack of pagination becomes a real latency problem per call, changeMasterPassword's single commit risks STORE_TIMEOUT regularly, and keeping every vault's VaultRecord in process memory with no eviction risks exhausting memory outright.
advanced.production_improvements: Add pagination to listEntries (limit/cursor-based). Redesign changeMasterPassword to commit in batches with a trackable, resumable rotation state. Introduce an LRU-style eviction or lazy-load strategy for VaultRecord objects backed by a real database, instead of holding every vault in memory permanently.

question: Using only encrypt/decrypt from src/crypto.ts, implement a generic reencryptBlob(oldKey, newKey, blob) function that returns the same plaintext re-encrypted under a new key with a fresh IV -- this is exactly what changeMasterPassword already does inline for every entry and for the sharing private key.
answer_hinglish:
Yeh exercise asal mein `changeMasterPassword` mein already DO baar inline likha hua logic hai, bas generalize karna hai ek reusable function mein. manager.ts mein entries loop mein likha hai: `const body = this.decryptBody(oldKey, stored.blob); reEncrypted.set(stored.id, { ...stored, blob: encrypt(newKey, Buffer.from(JSON.stringify(body), "utf8")) })` -- aur private key ke liye: `encrypt(newKey, decrypt(oldKey, record.wrappedPrivateKey))`.

Generic version simple hai: `decrypt(oldKey, blob)` se plaintext Buffer nikalo, phir `encrypt(newKey, plaintext)` call karo. `encrypt()` khud har call par `randomBytes(IV_LENGTH)` se naya IV generate karta hai -- isliye fresh IV ki guarantee AUTOMATICALLY milti hai, caller ko kuch extra karne ki zaroorat nahi.

Important baat: agar `decrypt(oldKey, blob)` fail hoti hai (galat oldKey, ya tampered blob), yeh already `DECRYPTION_FAILED` PasswordManagerError throw karta hai -- is wrapper function ko apna error handling add karne ki zaroorat NAHI hai, kyunki decrypt() khud hi correctly fail karta hai.

Yeh pattern useful hai kahin bhi jahan 'same secret, naye key ke under' chahiye ho -- private key rotation, ya future mein koi aur encrypted field jo key-rotation ke saath migrate karna ho.
why_needed: Candidate ko dikhana hai ki woh existing code se ek reusable abstraction extract kar sakta hai, aur crypto.ts ke encrypt/decrypt ke behavior (auto-fresh-IV, auto-throw-on-tamper) ko correctly samajhta hai.
real_world_analogy: Ek document ko ek purani combination lock se khol ke, usi document ko ek NAYE combination lock mein daal dena -- lock khud fresh combination choose kar leta hai, tumhe bas sahi purana combination jaanna hai aur naya lock dena hai.
how_it_works: decrypt(oldKey, blob) returns the plaintext Buffer (or throws DECRYPTION_FAILED). encrypt(newKey, plaintext) generates a fresh random IV internally and returns a brand new EncryptedBlob under the new key.
in_this_project: This is the exact logic already inlined twice in src/manager.ts::changeMasterPassword -- once in the entries re-encryption loop, once for `rewrappedPrivateKey`.
advantages: Reuses crypto.ts's existing fresh-IV and tamper-detection behavior with zero new logic
Removes duplicated inline re-encryption code from changeMasterPassword's two call sites
Trivially testable: round-trip under the same key, and a wrong oldKey must throw DECRYPTION_FAILED
disadvantages: Does not batch multiple blobs -- a caller re-encrypting many entries still loops externally
Leaves the JSON.stringify/parse step for structured entry bodies to the caller, since this function only knows about raw Buffers
common_mistakes: Manually generating an IV and passing it to encrypt() instead of letting encrypt() generate it itself
Catching and swallowing the DECRYPTION_FAILED error instead of letting it propagate, hiding a genuine wrong-key bug
Forgetting that the plaintext must be re-serialized (JSON.stringify) if the blob holds structured data, not raw bytes
follow_up_questions: How would you adapt this to re-encrypt many blobs atomically, matching changeMasterPassword's all-or-nothing guarantee?
What should happen if reencryptBlob is called with the SAME key for both oldKey and newKey?
Why is it safe for encrypt() to always generate its own IV rather than accepting one from the caller?

question: Add a new mutating operation, archiveVault(sessionId), that must never run concurrently with changeMasterPassword's rotation -- following the EXACT claim-before-await shape claimEntryOp already uses for entries. Implement it.
answer_hinglish:
Yeh exercise bilkul `addEntry`/`updateEntry`/`deleteEntry` ke shape ko COPY karna hai ek NAYE resource (archive flag) ke liye, taaki yeh existing `rotating`/`pendingEntryOps` exclusion ke saath properly interact kare.

Shape teen parts mein hai: (1) SYNCHRONOUS claim, await se pehle -- yahan existing `claimEntryOp` ko REUSE karna sabse sahi hai, kyunki archive operation bhi same exclusion chahta hai jo entries already use karte hain (rotation ke saath conflict na ho). (2) Ek `await` jo store commit karta hai. (3) SYNCHRONOUS apply (success par in-memory state update) ya release (`finally` mein `pendingEntryOps--`, chahe commit succeed ho ya fail).

Main yahan `record.pendingEntryOps` KHUD ke counter ko reuse kar raha hoon (naya counter banane ke jagah) kyunki semantically yeh exactly wahi guarantee chahta hai jo entry-ops already claim karte hain: 'rotation ke saath simultaneously nahi chal sakta.' Agar archive apna ALAG counter banata, toh `changeMasterPassword` ko bhi update karna padta us naye counter ko check karne ke liye -- jabki existing counter reuse karna is invariant ko free mein extend kar deta.

Commit ke liye, VaultRecord mein ek naya field add karna padega (jaise `archived: boolean`), aur `commit()` ke `fields` parameter ko extend karna padega isko include karne ke liye -- jaisa comment manager.ts mein already kehta hai: 'Every field that can change is passed explicitly -- never read implicitly off record.'
why_needed: Candidate ko dikhana hai ki woh is project ka REUSABLE concurrency pattern samajhta hai aur usko ek NAYE resource type ke liye correctly extend kar sakta hai, bina naya, redundant exclusion mechanism invent kiye.
real_world_analogy: Ek factory mein ek naya machine add karte ho jo bhi EXISTING safety-lockout system use kare (jo already doosri machines use kar rahi hain), uske jagah ek NAYA, parallel safety system banane ke jagah -- taaki sab machines ek hi 'danger zone' rule follow karein.
how_it_works: claimEntryOp(record) (reused, unchanged) -> await commit(...) with an `archived: true` field -> on success, set record.archived = true; on any failure, the finally block still decrements pendingEntryOps so the claim is never leaked.
in_this_project: Models directly on src/manager.ts::claimEntryOp and the shape of ::addEntry's try/finally around its own commit.
advantages: Reuses the existing exclusion guarantee for free -- no new interaction with changeMasterPassword's rotation to reason about
Matches the project's established shape exactly, so it is immediately recognizable to anyone who knows claimEntryOp
The finally block guarantees the claim is released even if the commit throws, same as every other entry op
disadvantages: Reusing pendingEntryOps couples archiveVault's exclusion to entry-ops specifically, which may not always be semantically exact if archive should behave slightly differently
Extending commit()'s fields parameter and VaultRecord/PersistedVault for a new field touches several places at once
No version-based conflict detection like updateEntry has -- archiveVault as written does not detect a race against another archiveVault call specifically
common_mistakes: Putting an await before calling claimEntryOp, reopening the exact race the pattern exists to close
Forgetting the finally block, which would leave pendingEntryOps permanently incremented after a failed commit
Reading the archived flag off `record` implicitly inside commit() instead of passing it explicitly as a field, breaking the project's own stated invariant
follow_up_questions: Would you reuse pendingEntryOps or add a dedicated counter for archive operations, and why?
How would changeMasterPassword need to change, if at all, to respect an archived vault?
What test would you write to prove archiveVault and changeMasterPassword cannot both be in flight on the same vault?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: Reusing the existing pendingEntryOps counter (fast, consistent with the rest of the codebase) vs introducing a dedicated archivingOps counter (more precise semantically, but requires changeMasterPassword to also learn about this new counter, duplicating the exclusion logic).
advanced.failure_scenarios: If the finally block were omitted, a failed commit (e.g. STORE_TIMEOUT) would leave pendingEntryOps permanently incremented, and the vault would report VAULT_BUSY for every future rotation attempt forever -- exactly the class of bug this project's mutation checks (S6/S7) are designed to catch for the existing operations.
advanced.alternatives: A dedicated `archiving` boolean flag with its own exclusion check (mirroring `rotating` rather than `pendingEntryOps`) if archive should be mutually exclusive with entry operations too, not just rotation -- a design choice depending on what 'archived' is meant to mean for the vault.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: This claim pattern's cost is O(1) regardless of scale within one process; the real scaling concern is the same one every claim in this project has -- it only works correctly within a single process's memory, so a multi-instance deployment would need this claim reimplemented against a shared atomic store, same as claimEntryOp itself.
advanced.production_improvements: Add a dedicated test modeled on test/concurrency.test.ts's existing 'entry operation racing a master-password rotation' tests, specifically for archiveVault vs changeMasterPassword. Extend VaultExport and PersistedVault to carry the archived flag consistently, matching how sharingPublicKey/wrappedPrivateKey were threaded through when they were added.

question: Write a vitest test, using this project's FakeVaultStore helper, proving that when two devices delete the SAME entry at the same time, the loser gets UNKNOWN_ENTRY instead of a silent second no-op success.
answer_hinglish:
Yeh exercise asal mein ek REAL existing test ko reproduce karna hai -- `test/concurrency.test.ts` mein 'two devices deleting the SAME entry at the same time' describe block mein yeh already likha hua hai, aur isi scenario ko mutation check S16 ('the already-deleted re-check removed') catch karta hai. Isi se seekhna hai ki is project mein races kaise test hoti hain.

Setup: `FakeVaultStore` (test/helpers.ts) ka `persist()` khud resolve NAHI hota -- test control karta hai KAB resolve ho, taaki exact interleaving guaranteed ho. Dono devices (`phone`, `laptop`) same vault unlock karte hain, ek entry seed hoti hai aur commit hoti hai (`store.resolveNext()` se).

Phir dono `deleteEntry` calls EK SAATH shuru hoti hain -- `const fromPhone = manager.deleteEntry(phone.sessionId, entry.id); const fromLaptop = manager.deleteEntry(laptop.sessionId, entry.id);`. Dono apna `claimEntryOp` synchronously le lete hain (koi conflict yahan nahi, delete entries ke against claim nahi hai). `await flush()` ke baad `store.pending` mein DONO commits honi chahiye.

Phir `store.resolveAt(0)` TWICE call karo -- phone ka commit pehle lands (entry actually remove hoti hai), phir laptop ka commit (jo ab ek already-gone entry par land karta hai). Assertion: `fromPhone` resolves undefined, `fromLaptop` rejects `UNKNOWN_ENTRY` -- yeh deleteEntry ke us RE-CHECK ko exercise karta hai jo commit ke BAAD check karta hai `if (!record.entries.has(entryId))`.
why_needed: Candidate ko dikhana hai ki woh is project ki race-testing technique (FakeVaultStore ke saath manual interleaving control) ko samajhta hai aur reproduce kar sakta hai, na ki sirf padh ke samajhta hai.
real_world_analogy: Do log EK SAATH ek document shred karne ki koshish karte hain -- pehla waqai shred kar deta hai, doosre ko pata chal jaata hai ki document already gaya hai, isliye woh 'already shredded' error paata hai, confusing silent success nahi.
how_it_works: deleteEntry's claim (claimEntryOp) does not conflict between two deletes of the same entry -- both proceed to their own commit. The post-commit re-check `if (!record.entries.has(entryId))` is what distinguishes the winner (entry still present at that point) from the loser (entry already removed by the winner's commit).
in_this_project: This exact test already exists: test/concurrency.test.ts, describe('two devices deleting the SAME entry at the same time'). The mutation it defends against is S16 in README's mutation-checks table.
advantages: Proves a specific documented race (S16 in README's mutation table) is actually caught, not just assumed
Uses the project's own FakeVaultStore pattern for deterministic interleaving, no real timing/sleeping needed
Mirrors an existing, real test exactly -- a good template for writing similar race tests for new operations
disadvantages: Does not by itself prove the entry was never double-counted anywhere else (e.g. in a separate index), only that deleteEntry's own return values are correct
Relies on manually controlling resolveAt ordering, which is easy to get subtly wrong (off-by-one in call order) when writing a new test
common_mistakes: Resolving the store calls in the WRONG order and accidentally testing a different interleaving than intended
Forgetting the seed add's own breach-check await step (flush()) before resolving its commit, causing store.pending to have the wrong length
Asserting only that one call rejects, without also asserting the OTHER call actually succeeded (both outcomes matter)
follow_up_questions: What would this test need to look like for two concurrent updateEntry calls on the same entry instead of two deletes?
Why does deleteEntry's claim (claimEntryOp) not itself prevent two deletes of the same entry from both proceeding?
How would you adapt this test to prove an update racing a delete gets UNKNOWN_ENTRY, not ENTRY_CONFLICT?

question: generatePassword's SYMBOLS pool can produce characters easily confused on-screen or on some keyboards (like 0/O or 1/l/I in the alphanumeric pools). Add an excludeAmbiguous option that removes commonly-confused characters from whichever pools are enabled, without breaking the existing 'at least one character per enabled pool' guarantee.
answer_hinglish:
generator.ts mein abhi `LOWER`, `UPPER`, `DIGITS`, `SYMBOLS` four fixed pools hain, aur logic do steps mein chalta hai: (1) har ENABLED pool se kam se kam ek character guarantee karna, (2) baaki length ko `fullCharset` (sab enabled pools ka join) se randomly fill karna, phir Fisher-Yates shuffle.

Ambiguous characters remove karne ke liye sabse clean approach: pools ko filter karna EXCLUDE-list ke against, BEFORE unhe `pools` array mein push karna -- taaki existing 'guarantee one per pool' logic bilkul waisa hi chale, bas pools ka content chhota hoga.

Ek IMPORTANT edge case: agar koi pool filter karne ke baad EMPTY ho jaaye (jaise agar DIGITS se 0 aur 1 hata do aur koi doosra digit enabled na ho... yahan actually DIGITS mein 8 characters bachenge, toh empty nahi hoga, par general case mein yeh check zaroori hai) -- existing `if (pools.length === 0)` check already is case ko partially cover karta hai agar SAB pools empty ho jaayein, par ek INDIVIDUAL pool empty hone se bhi guard karna chahiye, warna `pool[randomInt(pool.length)]` crash karega (`randomInt(0)` invalid hai).

Tumhe `MIN_GENERATED_LENGTH` ke saath bhi dhyaan rakhna hai -- woh already check karta hai length >= enabled-pools-count, par agar koi pool empty filter ho jaaye, toh effective pool count kam ho sakta hai, isliye woh guarantee bhi recompute karni padegi.
why_needed: Candidate ko dikhana hai ki woh existing, well-tested code (generatePassword) ko safely extend kar sakta hai bina uske existing invariants (guaranteed-per-class, shuffle) todte hue, aur edge cases (empty pool after filtering) identify kar sakta hai.
real_world_analogy: Ek recipe mein kuch ingredients allergy ki wajah se hata rahe ho -- baaki recipe ka process (mix karna, bake karna) same rehta hai, bas tumhe check karna padta hai ki koi ek category ingredient-less na ho jaaye poori tarah.
how_it_works: Filter each enabled pool's character string against an AMBIGUOUS set before pushing it into `pools`, keeping the rest of generatePassword (guaranteed-one-per-pool, fill, Fisher-Yates shuffle) unchanged; guard against a pool becoming empty after filtering.
in_this_project: Builds directly on src/generator.ts::generatePassword's existing pools array and its `pools.push(...)` / `fullCharset` / guaranteed-one-per-class loop.
advantages: Reuses the existing guaranteed-one-per-pool and shuffle logic untouched
Opt-in (defaults to false), so no existing caller or test behavior changes
Guards against a pool becoming empty after filtering, avoiding a randomInt(0) crash
disadvantages: Slightly reduces the effective character space, which for a fixed length modestly lowers entropy
The 'at least one from each pool' guarantee now depends on the filtered pool being non-empty, adding one more edge case to test
Hardcoded ambiguous-character set may not match every font/use case a caller cares about
common_mistakes: Filtering the pools AFTER already computing fullCharset, leaving stale unfiltered characters in the fill step
Forgetting to guard against an individual pool becoming empty after filtering, causing randomInt(0) to throw
Changing MIN_GENERATED_LENGTH's meaning instead of just adjusting which pools are eligible
follow_up_questions: What test would you add to prove excludeAmbiguous never produces a 0, O, 1, l, or I in the output?
What should happen if excludeAmbiguous is true and it empties every enabled pool?
Would you make the ambiguous character set configurable, or keep it fixed?

question: README's 'Known and NOT handled' section says there is no rate limiting at the HTTP layer independent of the library's own lockout. Implement a simple per-API-key token-bucket rate-limiting Express middleware, and say exactly where in createApp's middleware chain it should go.
answer_hinglish:
README explicitly likhta hai: 'The HTTP API has no CORS, no per-end-user session/cookie layer, and no rate limiting of its own' aur 'No rate limiting independent of the vault.' Abhi `createApp` ka middleware chain hai: auth check (`app.use` jo `keyMatches` check karta hai) -> `express.json()` body parser -> routes.

Token-bucket rate limiter ka core idea: har caller (yahan ek API key, future multi-tenant mein ek tenantId) ke paas ek 'bucket' hai jisme tokens hain; har request EK token consume karti hai; bucket slowly REFILL hota hai time ke saath ek fixed rate par. Agar bucket empty hai, request reject ho jaati hai (429 Too Many Requests).

Isko RIGHT AFTER auth middleware lagana chahiye, BEFORE `express.json()` -- is tarah se ek rate-limited caller ka body abhi parse hi nahi hoga (same reasoning jo auth middleware already follow karta hai: 'an unauthenticated caller gets 401 before its body is even parsed'). Rate limiting bhi isi reasoning ko follow karti hai: ek over-limit caller ka body parse karna bhi wasted work hai.

Implementation ke liye ek simple in-memory Map<apiKeyHash, {tokens, lastRefillAt}> kaafi hai is project ke scope ke liye (jaisa existing lockout bhi in-memory hai) -- production mein yeh Redis mein jaana chahiye agar multiple instances ho (same reasoning jo sessions/shares ke liye hai).
why_needed: Candidate ko dikhana hai ki woh is project ke existing middleware chain ko samajhta hai aur usme ek NAYI, well-known resilience pattern (token bucket) ko correctly integrate kar sakta hai, sahi jagah par.
real_world_analogy: Ek water tank (bucket) jisme paani (tokens) ek fixed rate par refill hota hai -- tum jab chaho paani nikaal sakte ho jab tak tank mein ho, par agar tank khaali hai toh wait karna padta hai jab tak thoda refill na ho.
how_it_works: Each request: compute elapsed time since lastRefillAt, add elapsed*refillRate tokens (capped at bucket capacity), then if tokens >= 1, consume one and allow; else reject with 429.
in_this_project: Would sit in src/http/app.ts::createApp's middleware chain, right after the existing auth `app.use` and before `express.json()` -- mirroring the project's own reasoning for why auth runs before body parsing.
advantages: Placed after auth and before body parsing, matching this project's own 'reject cheaply before doing more work' pattern
Per-API-key buckets mean one caller being rate-limited does not affect another
Token bucket naturally allows short bursts while still enforcing a steady-state rate
disadvantages: In-memory buckets do not survive a restart and are per-process, same limitation as sessions/shares at multi-instance scale
Keying by the raw Authorization header string (rather than a hashed/validated key) could be refined for safety and memory bounding
No automatic cleanup of buckets for keys that stop being used, which could leak memory over a very long uptime
common_mistakes: Placing the rate limiter AFTER express.json(), wasting body-parsing work on requests that will be rejected anyway
Forgetting to cap tokens at `capacity` after refill, letting a long-idle bucket accumulate unbounded tokens
Rate limiting globally instead of per-key, letting one noisy caller exhaust the limit for everyone
follow_up_questions: How would this rate limiter need to change for the multi-tenant API-key design discussed elsewhere in this bank?
What happens to this rate limiter's correctness if the app runs as multiple instances behind a load balancer?
Would you rate limit per-route differently (e.g. stricter on /vaults/:ownerId/unlock) rather than one global limit?

advanced.architecture_tradeoffs: An in-process token bucket is simple and has zero added runtime dependency, matching this project's existing style, but it only rate-limits per-process -- correctness across multiple instances requires a shared store (Redis with atomic INCR/Lua scripts), which is a materially bigger dependency to take on just for rate limiting.
advanced.failure_scenarios: If buckets are kept in memory with no eviction, a deployment with many distinct API keys over a long uptime could accumulate unbounded bucket entries, a slow memory leak; at multi-instance scale without a shared store, a caller could get up to N times the intended rate limit by spreading requests across N instances, each with its own full bucket.
advanced.alternatives: A fixed-window or sliding-window counter instead of token bucket (simpler, but allows bursting at window boundaries); a Redis-backed token bucket (correct across instances, at the cost of a new dependency and network round trip per request); or rate limiting entirely at an API gateway/reverse proxy layer, outside this application's code.
advanced.scale_10x_100x: At 10x traffic from a modest number of distinct API keys, the in-memory map stays small and cheap. At 100x traffic or a large number of distinct keys (e.g. in the multi-tenant redesign), the in-memory map needs an eviction policy (LRU or TTL) to stay bounded, and multi-instance deployments need the shared-store version to enforce a consistent limit per key across all instances.
advanced.production_improvements: Add TTL-based eviction for idle buckets. Move bucket state to Redis for correctness across multiple instances. Differentiate rate limits per route (e.g. a stricter limit on /vaults/:ownerId/unlock, which touches the lockout-sensitive path, versus a looser limit on read-only routes).
